Q3480
Retina & Vitreous
What diagnostic test is most helpful in assessing hemorrhagic choroidal detachment?
Correct answer: A. B-scan echography
Rationale
In the setting of a hemorrhagic choroidal detachment, B-scan echography is the most useful test. Hemorrhagic choroidal detachments are often associated with vitreous hemorrhage, which can prevent ophthalmoscopic assessment. Additionally, B-scan echography can determine whether the suprachoroidal clots have liquefied over time, facilitating their drainage.
Fluorescein angiography does not address the peripheral topography where hemorrhagic choroidals develop, and is useless in the setting of significant vitreous hemorrhage.
Optical coherence tomography can demonstrate choroidal thickening, but is useless in the periphery and through moderate to dense vitreous opacification.
The ERG may be reduced by hemorrhagic choroidal detachment, and is less affected by the vitreous hemorrhage, but does not address the important clinical issues of topography, associated exudative versus rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, or clot liquefaction.

Q3481
Retina & Vitreous
An 18-year-old man develops a quadrantic, inferotemporal, fovea-threatening retinal detachment with associated retinal dialysis. What is the best management option?
Correct answer: B. scleral buckle
Rationale
The one-operation anatomic success rate for a scleral buckle procedure in this setting exceeds 90%. Pars plana vitrectomy, retinopexy, and postoperative gas tamponade would induce a cataract in this 18-year-old patient that could be avoided with a scleral buckle procedure. The anatomic success rate for a pneumatic retinopexy procedure for this inferior retinal break would be unacceptably low. Cryopexy alone is not indicated for a fovea-threatening retinal detachment.

Q3482
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most likely causative organism of endogenous endophthalmitis associated with diabetic liver abscess?
Correct answer: D. Klebsiella species
Rationale
Klebsiella species

Klebsiella species is the most common cause of endogenous endophthalmitis in patients with liver abscesses.
Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species are the most common causes of endogenous endophthalmitis in patients with endocarditis.
Escherichia coli is a common cause of endogenous endophthalmitis in patients with urinary tract infections.

Q3483
Retina & Vitreous
Shortly after cataract surgery a patient develops persistent, symptomatic decrease in acuity in the operated eye. A fluorescein angiogram of the patient’s retina is shown. Treatment with topical ketorolac was ineffective. What treatment should be considered next?
Correct answer: A. periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid therapy
Rationale
The image demonstrates angiographic cystoid macular edema. This most commonly occurs after otherwise uncomplicated cataract surgery. The edema may resolve spontaneously or respond to the administration of topical steroidal and nonsteroidal therapy. Of the treatments listed, periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid therapy represents the most effective treatment for persistent cases. Less commonly, pars plana vitrectomy may be indicated to address specific associated complications such as retained crystalline lens fragments or demonstrated foveal traction. The other treatments listed have no known value in treating postoperative CME.

Q3484
Retina & Vitreous
What condition is a complication of pathologic myopia (myopic degeneration)?
Correct answer: A. foveal atrophy
Rationale
Foveal atrophy can occur as a complication of pathologic myopia (myopic degeneration). Choroidal effusion and folds are associated more with hyperopia than myopia. Juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasia is not closely associated with refractive error or axial length.

Q3485
Retina & Vitreous
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism underlying most cases of choroidal rupture?
Correct answer: C. indirect concussive injury to the posterior pole
Rationale
The pathophysiologic mechanism underlying most cases of choroidal rupture is an indirect concussive injury to the posterior pole. Because this is the result of blunt trauma, there is no penetration of the choroid by a foreign body. As these ruptures occur immediately at the time of injury, inflammation has not yet developed. Ingrowth of neovascular tissue can occur at the site of a choroidal rupture, but this does not cause the rupture.

Q3486
Retina & Vitreous
A 14-year-old boy with juvenile retinoschisis presents with sudden-onset of floaters in his right eye.  What is the mostly likely reason for the floaters to develop?
Correct answer: D. He has a vitreous hemorrhage.
Rationale
In juvenile retinoschisis, the splitting of retina occurs in the nerve fiber layer. Retinal splitting in deeper layers occurs in degenerative (senile) retinoschisis. About 50% of patients with juvenile retinoschisis develop peripheral retinoschisis. Boys with juvenile retinoschisis often present with vitreous hemorrhages secondary to torn retinal vessels in areas of retinoschisis. The causative gene is located on the X chromosome.

Q3487
Retina & Vitreous
What study demonstrated that intensive glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus reduced complications?
Correct answer: B. United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS)
Rationale
The UKPDS showed that intensive glycemic control in type 2 diabetes reduced rates of retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. Similarly, the DCCT showed reduced complication rates in type 1 diabetes under strict glycemic control. The ACCORD study raised concerns regarding intensive glucose control in patients with type 2 diabetes, given the increased risk of cardiovascular mortality suggested by the study results. The DPP demonstrated that moderate walking could reduce the risk of progression from impaired glucose tolerance to type 2 diabetes.

Q3488
Retina & Vitreous
What condition is a relative contraindication to performing fluorescein angiography (FA)?
Correct answer: B. pregnancy
Rationale
Although no serious adverse events have been reported to occur in pregnancy with FA, it is considered a contraindication to FA. Also, fluorescein is transmitted to breast milk in lactating women.
Fluorescein undergoes renal, not hepatic, elimination. Diabetes mellitus and anemia are not affected by intravenous sodium fluorescein.

Q3489
Retina & Vitreous
A 36-year-old woman presents with decreased vision and photopsias in the right eye. An automated visual field showed temporal field abnormalities and an enlarged blind-spot. The fluorescein angiogram is shown below. What is this condition?
Correct answer: D. multiple evanescent white dot syndrome
Rationale
Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome angiography is characterized by wreath-like clusters of punctate hyperfluorescence associated with spots observed clinically. Temporal field loss and an enlarged blind spot are common.
Fluorescein angiography (FA) of acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy lesions typically demonstrates early blockage followed by late leakage and staining.
Birdshot uveitis typically shows leakage from the retinal vessels and optic nerve head, frequently producing cystoid macular edema.
Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy angiography may show retinal or optic nerve head capillary leakage. FA images tend to be normal early on, then become abnormal in eyes with retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) alterations.

Q3490
Retina & Vitreous
Where is the vitreous most firmly attached to intraocular tissue?
Correct answer: A. vitreous base
Rationale
Vitreous is attached to the basal lamina of the lens, optic nerve, and retina and fills the vitreous cavity of the eye. It is most tightly adherent at the vitreous base, where the vitreous remains firmly adherent to the retina. This attachment is so strong that it can lead to vitreous base avulsion after severe trauma. With age, the vitreous contracts and can result in a posterior vitreous detachment. With this contraction, the posterior cortical gel detaches toward the firmly attached vitreous base.

Q3491
Retina & Vitreous
What clinical finding is considered a risk factor for the development of neovascular age-related macular degeneration?
Correct answer: C. large drusen with pigment clumping
Rationale
According to the Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS), stage 2 (multiple small or few intermediate drusen in 1 or both eyes) of the dry form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) had a very low incidence of progression to neovascular AMD, whereas stage 3 (a few large drusen or multiple intermediate drusen) and stage 4 (geographic atrophy) eyes had high incidences of progression to neovascular AMD after 5 years (18% for stage 3, and 40% for stage 4). Pigment clumping was considered an additional risk factor according to AREDS.

Q3492
Retina & Vitreous
What property of indocyanine green allows for imaging of the choroidal vasculature?
Correct answer: A. It is almost completely protein bound after intravenous injection.
Rationale
Indocyanine green angiography is useful because it is able to delineate deeper structures in the choroid, since the tricarbocyanine dye is almost completely protein bound (98%). This is in contrast to fluorescein, which freely diffuses. ICG is water-soluble. ICG's excitation and emissions peaks are in the near-infrared range.

Q3493
Retina & Vitreous
An ophthalmologist decides to perform photodynamic therapy (PDT) for a 35-year-old man with chronic central serous chorioretinopathy. Half-fluence rather than standard-fluence PDT may reduce the risk of what potential complication?
Correct answer: A. choroidal ischemia
Rationale
Photodynamic therapy (PDT) utilizes local laser activation of the photosensitizing drug verteporfin to generate reactive oxygen species and free radicals that damage endothelial cells and ultimately lead to vascular thrombosis. Ophthalmic complications encountered after PDT include transient visual loss, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, choroidal ischemia, and choroidal neovascularization. Measures to mitigate these complications have included using half-fluence PDT, in which 25 J/cm2 rather than 50 J/cm2 is applied. Patients are vulnerable to cutaneous photosensitivity reactions after treatment that can result in mild to second degree burns of exposed skin, and they are thus advised to minimize their exposure to sunlight for 5 days after treatment. A small percentage of patients reports transient lower back, side, and chest pain after verteporfin infusion. Choroidal detachment can occur after extensive laser photocoagulation but is not a complication of PDT.

Q3494
Retina & Vitreous
For the condition shown in the photograph, what surgical intervention would be preferred?
Correct answer: D. pars plana vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle
Rationale
The fundus findings shown are star folds from proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR), a complication of retinal detachment that occurs in 8% to 10% of cases. PVR is the most common cause of reattachment failure and warrants more aggressive treatment. Retinal detachment with PVR represents a combined tractional and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, which may necessitate both a scleral buckle and vitrectomy and/or other adjuncts to achieve attachment. Pars plana vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle is the most definitive surgical intervention for retinal detachment with PVR. Pneumatic retinopexy is contraindicated in the presence of proliferative vitreoretinopathy as it cannot treat the tractional component and is typically unsuccessful. Retinal cryopexy and/or scleral buckling may be used in association with vitrectomy for the management of proliferative vitreoretinopathy, but likewise, these may not be as effective for PVR greater than stage C2 (2 quadrants of star folds).

Q3495
Retina & Vitreous
What is a function of the retinal pigment epithelium?
Correct answer: D. phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments
Rationale
Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments is a function of the retinal pigment epithelium. Functions of the retinal pigment epithelium also include the  absorption of light, vitamin A metabolism, formation of the outer blood retinal barrier, maintenance of the subretinal space, and healing of traumatic injuries.

Q3496
Retina & Vitreous
What part of the retina is affected by commotio retinae?
Correct answer: A. photoreceptor layer and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)
Rationale
Commotio retinae is retinal whitening caused by shock waves from blunt trauma. OCT shows disruption at the level of the photoreceptor layer and retinal pigment epithelium. It most commonly affects the posterior pole but can affect the peripheral retina.

Q3497
Retina & Vitreous
What ophthalmoscopic retinal finding is most characteristic of an exudative retinal detachment?
Correct answer: D. subretinal fluid that shifts with a change in patient position
Rationale
Subretinal fluid that shifts with a change in patient position is typical of an exudative retinal detachment. Retinal detachment with a taut concave surface is characteristic of a tractional retinal detachment, not an exudative retinal detachment. A corrugated appearance to the retina is most common with rhegmatogenous retinal detachments, while exudative retinal detachments usually have a smooth appearance. Fixed retinal folds typically indicate proliferative vitreoretinopathy, which is almost always secondary to a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Q3498
Retina & Vitreous
What percentage of patients with vitreous hemorrhage and an acute symptomatic posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) have a retinal tear?
Correct answer: A. 60%
Rationale
Noting the presence or absence of vitreous hemorrhage is a critical aspect of evaluating an acute PVD because of the relationship of this finding to retinal tears. Although retinal tears are reported in up to 18% of patients with acute symptomatic PVDs, the presence of vitreous hemorrhage raises the prevalence to between 50% and 70%. About 10% of patients without vitreous hemorrhage have retinal tears, so careful examination is mandated even in the absence of this clinical finding.

Q3499
Retina & Vitreous
What therapeutic intervention should be considered in the management of dominant (familial) drusen complicated by subfoveal choroidal neovascularization?
Correct answer: C. intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy
Rationale
Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) associated with familial or dominant drusen is responsive to anti-VEGF therapy. Grid laser photocoagulation has been shown to reduce drusen count and volume in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), but it is not effective in reducing the risk of CNV in AMD. External beam radiation therapy has been associated with the development of CNV. Plasmapheresis is not a treatment for CNV.

Q3500
Retina & Vitreous
What ciliopathy is associated with pigmentary retinopathy and hearing loss?
Correct answer: D. Usher syndrome
Rationale
Ciliopathies are diseases or syndromes in which a mutation in a gene needed for ciliary function affects multiple organ systems. Usher syndrome is a ciliopathy defined by the association of retinitis pigmentosa with congenital sensorineural hearing loss. Bardet-Biedl syndrome is a ciliopathy with findings that include pigmentary retinopathy and bull’s-eye maculopathy, obesity, polydactyly, hypogonadism, renal disease, and cognitive disability. Joubert syndrome is a ciliopathy characterized by cerebellar malformation (“molar tooth” sign) and hypotonia, with additional features that include retinal dystrophy and renal disease. Jeune syndrome is a retinal ciliopathy complicated by cystic kidney disease and asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy.

Q3501
Retina & Vitreous
A 22-year-old patient reports blurry vision and floaters. What is the most likely etiology?
Correct answer: D. idiopathic
Rationale
According to the Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group, intermediate uveitis is a subset of posterior uveitis wherein the vitreous is the major site of inflammation. Eighty percent (80%) of intermediate uveitis cases are idiopathic. The most commonly identified associations in North America and Europe are sarcoidosis and multiple sclerosis (MS).

Q3502
Retina & Vitreous
A 52-year-old man presents with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and tractional retinal detachment (TRD) involving the central macula. What is the appropriate management?
Correct answer: A. pars plana vitrectomy, retinal membrane removal
Rationale
The appropriate management of diabetic TRD involving or threatening the macula is pars plana vitrectomy, to eliminate vitreoretinal adhesion and subsequent traction in order to reattach the retina.
Panretinal photocoagulation should precede vitrectomy if possible, but panretinal photocoagulation alone is not the appropriate treatment. Pneumatic retinopexy is used to manage rhegmatogenous retinal detachments associated with breaks in the superior 8 clock-hours, and while diabetic tractional detachments can sometimes present with combined tractional/rhegmatogenous detachments (breaks in atrophic areas), pneumatic retinopexy would be inappropriate in this scenario.

Q3503
Retina & Vitreous
A 35-year-old man felt a sharp pain in his left eye while hammering a nail into a plank on his deck. His slit-lamp photograph is abnormal as shown. What test would be most useful to direct further management of this patient?
Correct answer: B. computed tomography (CT)
Rationale
The slit-lamp photograph depicts a small Seidel-positive corneal wound. Given the history of hammering metal-on-metal, you must search for or exclude the presence of an intraocular foreign body. A CT scan without contrast of the orbits is the best choice. For radiopaque materials, CT is superior to other imaging modalities for visualizing and localizing intraocular foreign bodies. In the hands of an experienced ultrasonographer, B scans are particularly useful for nonradiopaque materials. Heavy-handed use of the B scan ultrasound probe on a possible open globe could, however, lead to further injury. MRI would be contraindicated in a patient with a suspected metallic intraocular foreign body because the scan could cause the metal to migrate. Electroretinography can be used to look for late toxicity associated with a metallic foreign body but would not be needed in the acute phase.

Q3504
Retina & Vitreous
What is a clinical manifestation of bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation (BDUMP)?
Correct answer: C. serous retinal detachment
Rationale
BDUMP causes diffuse thickening of the choroid, reddish or brownish choroidal discoloration, serous retinal detachment, and cataracts. The bilateral proliferation of benign melanocytes is usually associated with or often heralds a systemic cancer. Common tumors associated with BDUMP are cancers of the ovary, uterus, and lung. BDUMP can also occur with cancers of the colon, pancreas, gallbladder, and esophagus.

Q3505
Retina & Vitreous
A premature infant has immature vascularization in zone I but no evidence of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) on initial screening examination. What is the appropriate interval for the next screening examination?
Correct answer: C. 1 week
Rationale
The follow-up interval for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) screening is determined based on the disease features; more severe disease indicates a need for shorter follow-up intervals. A premature infant with immature vascularization in zone I should be reevaluated in 1 week or less, even in the absence of ROP.
Screening Intervals
1-Week or Less Follow-up
  • immature vascularization: zone I—no ROP
  • immature retina extends into posterior zone II, near the boundary of zone I
  • stage 1 or 2 ROP: zone I
  • stage 3 ROP: zone II
  • the presence or suspected presence of aggressive posterior ROP
1-to 2-Week Follow-up
  • immature vascularization; posterior zone II
  • stage 2 ROP: zone II
  • unequivocally regressing ROP: zone I
2-Week Follow-up
  • stage 1 ROP: zone II
  • immature vascularization: zone II—no ROP
  • unequivocally regressing ROP: zone II
2- to 3-Week Follow-up
  • stage 1 or 2 ROP: zone III
  • regressing ROP: zone III

Q3506
Retina & Vitreous
A fluorescein angiogram (FA) is planned to evaluate vision loss in a patient who had a previous urticarial reaction to IV contrast dye. What preventative treatment should be considered?
Correct answer: C. antihistamine
Rationale
The most common side effects of FA are nausea and hives, each of which occurs in approximately 5% of patients. Nausea can be treated with an antiemetic, but will usually pass in a few seconds without treatment. Antihistamines are useful prophylactic treatment for urticaria. Epinephrine is used for anaphylactic reactions, and dantrolene is used for malignant hyperthermia.

Q3507
Retina & Vitreous
In what quadrant of the retina does degenerative retinoschisis typically present?
Correct answer: D. inferotemporal quadrant
Rationale
Degenerative retinoschisis is usually asymptomatic. It most commonly involves the peripheral retina and is best seen on scleral depression. The inferotemporal quadrant is most commonly affected. Degenerative retinoschisis tends to be bilateral in the majority of cases. The scotoma due to retinoschisis is an absolute scotoma.

Q3508
Retina & Vitreous
The Diabetic Retinopathy Vitrectomy Study demonstrated the efficacy of vitrectomy surgery to decrease significant vision loss (SVL) from what complication of diabetic retinopathy?
Correct answer: B. nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage
Rationale
The Diabetic Retinopathy Vitrectomy Study demonstrated the efficacy of vitrectomy surgery to treat vitreous hemorrhage complicating proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and combined with endolaser photocoagulation to treat the underlying proliferative diabetic retinopathy. The study did not demonstrate the efficacy of vitrectomy surgery to treat or prevent traction retinal detachment, macular edema, or intraretinal hemorrhage complicating PDR. The ETDRS looked at the treatment of CSME. Most ERD related to PRP will resolve without treatment or when treated with ocular or systemic steroids.

Q3509
Retina & Vitreous
Angioid streaks are associated with the deposition of what material in the Bruch membrane?
Correct answer: D. calcium
Rationale
Angioid streaks are linear small breaks in the Bruch membrane. They were first described by Doyne (1889) in a patient with retinal hemorrhages. Knapp (1892) called them "angioid streaks" because of their resemblance to blood vessels. The pathology of angioid streaks is a combination of elastic degeneration and pathologic calcification of the Bruch membrane. Angioid streaks are often associated with pseudoxanthoma elasticum, but also are described in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Paget disease of bone, sickle cell anemia, thalassemia, and other hemoglobinopathies. They can be associated with damage to the overlying retinal pigment epithelium.

Q3510
Retina & Vitreous
For a patient with lattice degeneration, in what circumstances should a prophylactic laser barricade be considered?
Correct answer: D. history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye
Rationale
Although only limited data are available, an 11-year follow-up study of patients with untreated lattice degeneration and no symptomatic tears showed that retinal detachment occurred in approximately 1% of cases. Thus, the presence of lattice, with or without atrophic holes, does not generally require prophylaxis in the absence of other risk factors or symptoms. Paving stone degeneration does not predispose to retinal detachment. If lattice degeneration is present in a patient with additional risk factors, such as retinal detachment in the fellow eye, flap tears, or aphakia, then prophylactic treatment can be considered. A phakic, hyperopic, or emmetropic eye is considered lower risk for retinal detachment and would not require laser barricade.

Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common setting in which Bacillus cereus endophthalmitis should be suspected?
Correct answer: D. post-traumatic endophthalmitis
Rationale
Bacillus cereus accounts for almost 25% cases of posttraumatic endophthalmitis. It rarely causes endophthalmitis in other settings.

Q3512
Retina & Vitreous
When should an infant be ophthalmoscopically screened for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?
Correct answer: D. Screening should be performed on all premature neonates with a birth weight of 1500 g or less, with a gestational age of 30 weeks or less before hospital discharge, or who have reached 4–6 weeks of age.
Rationale
Several risk factors have been associated with the development of ROP in premature neonates, including low birth weight, low gestational age, oxygen therapy, apnea, sepsis, and others. Premature infants with a birth weight of 1500 g or less, of gestational age of 30 weeks or less, or who require supplemental oxygen are particularly at risk of developing ROP. Initial examination of the peripheral retina by indirect ophthalmoscopy in these neonates (and in selected infants with a birth weight between 1500 and 2000 g or gestational age of >30 weeks with an unstable clinical course) is recommended before hospital discharge, or by 4–6 weeks of postnatal age (or within the 31st to 33rd week of postconceptional or postmenstrual age, whichever is later). Retinal exams are repeated every 1–2 weeks until the retina becomes fully vascularized or ROP is noted. If ROP develops, weekly exams should be performed to watch for possible progression to threshold disease.

Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) most commonly results from what linkage pattern?
Correct answer: C. sporadic
Rationale

Q3514
Retina & Vitreous
A 1-month-old baby is admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with bulging fontanelles, a spiral fracture of the femur and multiple skin bruises. What would be the most appropriate time for a fundus examination?
Correct answer: A. as soon as possible
Rationale
Retinal hemorrhages in abusive head trauma can begin to resolve very rapidly. Patients suspected of abusive head trauma should undergo a fundus examination on presentation or as soon as possible. It is not advisable to wait 2 to 3 weeks, or for discharge from the ICU or from the hospital.

Q3515
Retina & Vitreous
What condition or characteristic is most commonly associated with a retinal arterial macroaneurysm?
Correct answer: C. systemic hypertension
Rationale
Retinal arterial macroaneurysms are acquired ectasias of the retinal arterioles. They are associated with systemic arterial hypertension in approximately two-thirds of cases. They are more common in females than males, and in individuals more than 60 years old. There is no specific association between retinal arteriolar macroaneurysms and diabetes mellitus.

Q3516
Retina & Vitreous
What finding in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease suggests chronicity?
Correct answer: A. choroidal depigmentation, or "sunset glow" fundus
Rationale
Serous retinal detachment, optic disc hyperemia, and choroidal thickening are all signs of the acute uveitic phase of Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease. Choroidal depigmentation, or "sunset glow" fundus, is a sign of recurrent/chronic disease and occurs late in the course of the condition.

Q3517
Retina & Vitreous
A 64-year-old woman presents with visual loss 1 week after cataract extraction and intraocular lens implantation. She notes no ocular pain. Visual acuity is 20/100. A wound leak is present. A 2 mm hypopyon and moderate vitreous haze are present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. infectious endophthalmitis
Rationale
The clinical presentation is suggestive of postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis, and must be treated as such unless proven otherwise. Not all endophthalmitis is painful at the time of onset. The presence of a wound leak explains the later-than-average time of onset following surgery. Sympathetic ophthalmia occurs in response to a traumatized fellow eye, which is not part of the history in this case. Sterile inflammation (toxic anterior segment syndrome [TASS]) occurs immediately following surgery. This is not a typical presentation of intraocular lens-induced uveitis (uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema [UGH] syndrome), a rare condition.

Q3518
Retina & Vitreous
What is a common fundus finding in idiopathic central serous choroidopathy (ICSC)?
Correct answer: D. pigment epithelial detachment
Rationale
The characteristic lesion complex of idiopathic central serous chorioretinopathy is a fluid-filled pigment epithelial detachment ("classic PED") under a localized serous retinal detachment. The presence of confluent drusen, subretinal hemorrhage, or exudate, either in the retina or in the subretinal space, should lead to further investigation, as ICSC alone does not cause these. Either the diagnosis is incorrect or an ICSC-associated choroidal neovascularization should be suspected.

Q3519
Retina & Vitreous
What demographic characteristic is commonly associated with punctate inner choroidopathy?
Correct answer: B. young female myopes
Rationale
Punctate inner choroidopathy is most commonly diagnosed in young female myopes. There is no proven racial predilection for this disorder.

Q3520

What type of hemorrhage is most characteristic of Valsalva retinopathy?
Correct answer: D. sub-internal limiting membrane (ILM) hemorrhage
Rationale
Sub-ILM hemorrhage is typical of Valsalva retinopathy. A sudden rise in intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure (such as accompanies coughing, vomiting, lifting, or straining for a bowel movement) might raise intraocular venous pressure sufficiently to rupture small superficial capillaries in the macula. It is typically self-limiting, not requiring prompt surgical intervention, and has a good visual prognosis.

Q3521

A 27-year-old man presents for a routine eye exam. His best-corrected visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye with hyperopic correction. His pupils are normally reactive with no relative afferent pupillary defect. His left optic nerve appearance is shown below. What may be a complication of his condition?
Correct answer: A. retinal ischemia
Rationale
The fundus photograph shows a prepapillary arteriolar loop over the left optic disc. These prepapillary loops are most commonly asymptomatic but may be associated with retinal vascular occlusions, amaurosis fugax, or vitreous hemorrhage. Serous retinal detachments may be seen in optic pits. Glaucoma and optic atrophy are not associated with prepapillary vascular loops.

What is a posterior extension of the pars plana epithelium onto the retinal side of the ora serrata?
Correct answer: C. enclosed ora bay
Rationale
An enclosed ora bay is a posterior extension of the pars plana epithelium onto the retinal side of the ora serrata. A peripheral retinal excavation is thought to be a variant of lattice degeneration. A dentate process is an extension of retinal tissue extending anteriorly to the ora serrata. A meridional complex is a prominent thickening of retinal tissue that extends into the pars plana and is aligned with a ciliary process.

Q3523

What patient is an ideal candidate for treatment of a retinal detachment with pneumatic retinopexy?
Correct answer: B. phakic patient with macula-involving, superior detachment with a horseshoe tear at 10 o'clock
Rationale
Pneumatic retinopexy is most efficacious for the repair of retinal detachments with solitary or closely clustered retinal breaks located in the superior 8 clock-hours of the retinal periphery. The success rate declines in the management of retinal detachments with multiple retinal breaks in multiple quadrants or pathologies that increase the risk of multi-quadrant or small (ie, difficult to identify) tears. For example, post-traumatic, lattice degeneration-associated, and pseudophakic patients have somewhat lower likelihoods of reattachment. Contraindications for pneumatic retinopexy include retinal breaks in the inferior 4 clock-hours of the retinal periphery or the presence of significant traction that would limit the ability of the retina to settle against the choroid (ie, proliferative vitreoretinopathy).

What inheritance pattern is most commonly associated with congenital color deficiency?
Correct answer: C. X-linked recessive
Rationale
Congenital color defects may involve trichromatous color confusion, dichromatous color confusion, or monochromacy. The most common inheritance pattern in these conditions is X-linked recessive (deuteranomalous and protanomalous abnormalities and blue-cone monochromatism), which accounts for over 90% of congenital color defects.

Q3525
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most widely used topical antiseptic for intravitreal injections?
Correct answer: A. povidone iodine
Rationale
Povidone iodine is the most widely used topical antiseptic for intravitreal injections. The efficacy of povidone iodine in this setting has been demonstrated in multiple clinical trials and retrospective case series. Chlorhexidine gluconate and ethyl alcohol are toxic to the ocular surface and should not be utilized in this setting.
Strict aseptic technique, including managing the eyelid to prevent contamination from the margin and lashes, is recommended. The application of povidone-iodine, 5%, to the ocular surface for at least 60–90 seconds prior to injection is widely considered beneficial. Antibiotic eyedrop use before or after injections is controversial and is not recommended in routine procedures, particularly given that repeat topical antibiotic application results in the development of resistant ocular flora.

Q3526
Retina & Vitreous
What medication can be associated with the development or exacerbation of macular edema?
Correct answer: D. pioglitazone
Rationale
Rosiglitazone and pioglitazone are oral hypoglycemics used in diabetic patients. They are occasionally associated with the development of or worsening of macular edema.
Thioridazine is a phenothiazine, which can cause pigmentary retinopathy when used in high doses. Onset can be within a few weeks of initial dosing. Vision can improve with treatment discontinuation.
Digitalis is known for causing xanthopsia, or yellow tinting of vision. Similarly, sildenafil and other phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors can cause a transient blue tint to vision.

Five years before developing moderately severe panuveitis in his operated eye, a 78-year-old white man underwent uncomplicated cataract surgery. What feature of his presentation is least consistent with the diagnosis of sympathetic ophthalmia?
Correct answer: B. unilaterality
Rationale
Sympathetic ophthalmia is always bilateral. Bilaterality might be difficult or impossible to document if the inciting eye is phthisical or has been removed. Sympathetic ophthalmia can occur in any race at any age and anytime following eye surgery or trauma.

Q3528
Retina & Vitreous
An 8-year-old boy presents with decreased vision since birth. His visual acuity is 20/200 OU and his electroretinogram (ERG) shows a negative waveform. His fundus examination is shown in the figure. What is most typical ophthalmoscopic finding in this condition?
Correct answer: B. macular radiating retinal folds
Rationale
The clinical presentation is consistent with X-linked retinoschisis (XLRS). Pediatric patients can present with foveal schisis, appearing as small cystoid spaces and radiating striae in the central macula. Parafoveal white spots are another presenting sign. In up to 50% of patients, peripheral retinoschisis may occur, and pigmentary changes with can mimic retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
By definition, no male-to-male transmission occurs in X-linked disease, and the patient's mother is an obligate carrier of a retinoschisin-1 (RS1) gene mutation. The patient's brother thus has a 50% chance of being affected with this disease, and his sister has a 50% chance of being a carrier. With regard to the patient's future children, his daughters will be obligate carriers and his sons will be unaffected. The risk to his grandchildren thus depends upon whether their mother or father is the patient's child: The sons of a carrier daughter have a 50% chance of having the condition. The percentage of affected grandchildren thus cannot be predicted based solely on the patient's condition. Identifying female carriers of X-linked diseases is important, given the potential risk to their children.

Q3529
Retina & Vitreous
What is a common cause of commotio retinae?
Correct answer: B. closed-globe blunt trauma
Rationale
Commotio retinae is damage to outer retinal layers caused by shock waves that traverse the eye from the site of impact following blunt trauma.
Penetrating injury to the globe typically reduces the intraocular pressure acutely, which reduces shock wave transmission. Commotio is rarely seen in this setting. High-velocity projectiles to the orbit cause retinitis sclopetaria, but unless the globe is compressed by a glancing projectile, commotio is rare. Crushing injury to bones is associated with Purtscher retinopathy.

What is the most likely etiology of the macular disease illustrated in the figure?
Correct answer: B. idiopathic
Rationale
This etiology for most full-thickness macular holes is not well understood; therefore, most are classified due to an idiopathic cause. When associated with functional visual impairment, pars plana vitrectomy surgery with posterior hyaloid dissection, with or without internal limiting membrane removal, and with postoperative gas tamponade, would be preferred in most situations. Less commonly, macular holes may occur following blunt trauma. Macular holes are not directly associated with diabetes mellitus or sun gazing.

Correct answer: A. behind the muscle insertions
Rationale
The sclera is the thinnest behind the insertions of the rectus muscles (0.3 mm). It is the thickest by the optic nerve head (1 mm). Clinically, it is important to remember the significant thinning of the sclera behind the rectus muscles when performing strabismus surgery.

What physiologic abnormality is associated with the pathophysiology of diabetic retinopathy?
Correct answer: C. vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) upregulation
Rationale
VEGF upregulation is associated with the pathophysiology of diabetic retinopathy. Retinal capillary basement membrane thickening, increased platelet adhesion, and retinal capillary pericyte loss are also associated with the pathophysiology of diabetic retinopathy.

Q3533

What is a characteristic aspect of familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR)?
Correct answer: D. failure of the temporal retina to vascularize
Rationale
FEVR is characterized by failure of the temporal retina to vascularize. Although it is phenotypically similar to ROP, patients are born full term and have normal respiratory status. Differentiation of FEVR from ROP is also aided by the family history and careful exam of all family members.

Q3534
Retina & Vitreous
What percentage of patients with type 1 diabetes will have some degree of diabetic retinopathy at 20 years or more after diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. >90%
Rationale
In type 1 diabetes (insulin dependent), insulin deficiency is secondary to an autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells. The etiology is thought to be multifactorial, with a genetic susceptibility triggered by environmental factors and certain viral infections (cytomegalovirus [CMV], measles, mumps, rubella, enterovirus, and parvovirus). The prevalence of diabetic retinopathy is 50% by 7 years after diagnosis. The prevalence increases to 90% in patients who have had type 1 diabetes for 15 or more years.

In the Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy, after 20 years of diabetes mellitus, nearly 99% of patients with type 1 disease and 60% of those with type 2 disease showed some degree of diabetic retinopathy.

Q3535
Retina & Vitreous
What electrophysiologic diagnostic study serves as a direct measure of central retinal ganglion cell function?
Correct answer: C. pattern electroretinogram (PERG)
Rationale
The pattern electroretinogram (PERG) is the retinal response to an isoluminant alternating checkerboard stimulus presented to the macula. The stimulus is primarily alternating contrast stimulus. The responses are small, and signal averaging is needed. There are 2 main components, P50 and N95, with most subjects showing an earlier negative component, N35. N95 arises in the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and thus acts as a direct measure of central RGC function.

The electro-oculogram (EOG) assesses the health of the RPE by measuring the changes in the corneo-retinal standing potential during light adaptation.

The multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) can be of use in the diagnosis of macular dysfunction and in assessing the extent of central retinal involvement in generalized retinal disease by producing a topographic electroretinogram (ERG) map of central retinal cone-system function.

The visual evoked potential (VEP), or visual evoked response (VER), is a measurement of the electrical signals produced in the brain in response to light stimulus, recorded at the scalp over the occipital cortex; it is a measure of the integrity of the afferent visual pathway.

Q3536
Retina & Vitreous
Anterior chamber reaction, iris neovascularization, and midperipheral intraretinal hemorrhages are suggestive of what clinical entity?
Correct answer: C. ocular ischemia
Rationale
Ocular ischemic syndrome results from hypoperfusion of the entire eye and sometimes the orbit, usually because of carotid artery obstruction. Patients present with decreased vision and mild ocular pain. Examination findings may include corneal edema, anterior chamber cells, and moderate flare, the latter often greater than and out of proportion to the number of cells Anterior segment neovascularization may be present. IOP may be low from decreased aqueous production due to ischemia or high due to neovascular glaucoma. A cataract may be more prominent on the involved side. The vitreous is usually clear. Dilated fundus examination may show mild disc edema associated with dilated retinal venules, narrowed arterioles, and medium to large intraretinal scattered blot hemorrhages in the midperiphery and far periphery of the retina. Neovascularization may be present on the disc or elsewhere in the retina. Fluorescein angiography shows delayed arteriolar filling, diffuse leakage in the posterior pole as well as from the optic disc, and signs of capillary nonperfusion.

Q3537
Retina & Vitreous
A 22-year-old man presents with bilateral vision loss. Vision is 20/400 and intraocular pressure is 15 mm Hg in both eyes, without an afferent pupillary defect. On examination, he has bilateral optic disc edema, intraretinal hemorrhages, and cotton wool spots. What is the most appropriate procedure to perform next?
Correct answer: B. blood pressure measurement
Rationale
First and foremost, the patient's blood pressure has to be checked to rule out malignant hypertension, which may be especially commonly found in young African American males. The most commonly observed diseases that lead to choroidal vascular compromise are those that cause severe, acute elevations in blood pressure, such as in malignant hypertension, eclampsia, or severe cocaine abuse.
Ocular effects of hypertension can be observed in the retina, choroid, and optic nerve. Retinal changes can be described and classified using ophthalmoscopy and angiography. Recognition of the posterior segment vascular changes by the ophthalmologist may prompt the initial diagnosis of hypertension and alert the patient to potential complications from this condition.

Q3538
Retina & Vitreous
On initial examination of a patient with a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), the ophthalmologist identifies pigment in the anterior vitreous. What additional finding during this examination increases the likelihood of discovering a retinal break?
Correct answer: A. vitreous hemorrhage
Rationale
About 7%-18% of all patients with acute symptomatic PVD have a retinal tear, and 50%-70% of PVD patients who have associated vitreous hemorrhage have retinal tears. The presence of pigment granules in the anterior vitreous ("tobacco dust") is associated with a 7-fold increase in the likelihood of finding a retinal tear. PVD usually starts a perifoveal detachment and then spreads circumferentially. A prominent Weiss ring has no bearing on the likelihood of a retinal break, nor does the presence of vitreous syneresis (which precedes PVD), or asteroid hyalosis.

Q3539
Retina & Vitreous
What term best describes the vision loss in cone dystrophy?
Correct answer: D. hemeralopia
Rationale
Patients with cone dystrophy present with progressive loss of visual acuity and color discrimination, often accompanied by hemeralopia (day blindness) and photophobia (discomfort and/or pain in the presence of normal levels of light). Onset of symptoms typically occurs in the teenage years or later adulthood. Ophthalmoscopy may be normal early in the course of the disease. Because of this, patients with cone dystrophies may be suspected of malingering. In other patients, ophthalmoscopy may reveal the typical symmetric bull’s-eye pattern of macular atrophy, or more severe atrophy, such as demarcated circular macular lesions. Mild to severe temporal optic atrophy and tapetal retinal reflexes (with a glistening greenish or golden sheen) may also be present. Unlike macular dystrophies, the cone dystrophies are more associated with color discrimination symptoms and photophobia, and as such, they must be differentiated from color vision defects. In rod dystrophy, patients complain of nyctalopia, or difficulty seeing in a dark or mesopic environment. Tunnel vision is associated with rod dysfunction (retinitis pigmentosa) and glaucoma.

Q3540
Retina & Vitreous
West Nile virus retinopathy is caused by a member of what class of virus?
Correct answer: C. flavivirus
Rationale
West Nile virus (WNV) retinopathy is caused by a member of the RNA flavivirus family. The disorder presents as curvilinearly arranged or scattered circular, deep, creamy chorioretinal inflammatory lesions. Inactive lesions are atrophic and partially pigmented, with a targetoid appearance. There is no proven treatment for WNV infection. In the majority of cases, the ocular disease is self-limited and the visual acuity returns to baseline. Complications may include chorioretinal scars, choroidal neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, ischemic maculopathy, and optic atrophy.
The herpesvirus family includes herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella zoster virus (VZV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), which can all cause inflammation in both the anterior and posterior segments. The adenovirus family is most commonly associated with epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and follicular conjunctivitis. The most common virus in the poxvirus family is molluscum contagiosum, which produces umbilicated nodules on the skin, eyelid margin, and conjunctiva.

What is a known risk factor for degenerative retinoschisis?
Correct answer: A. hyperopia
Rationale
Degenerative retinoschisis is commonly associated with hyperopia.
Lattice degeneration is more common in myopic eyes.
Collagen vascular disease and prior retinal detachment do not increase the risk of degenerative retinoschisis.

Q3542

What is the preferred treatment for stage 4 retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?
Correct answer: C. lens-sparing vitrectomy
Rationale
Eyes with stage 4 ROP (progressive, active-phase ROP) require surgical intervention using scleral buckling or a lens-sparing vitrectomy to alleviate the vitreoretinal traction causing retinal detachment. Eyes undergoing surgical intervention at stage 4A—rather than at later stages 4B or 5—have more favorable outcomes. Lens-sparing vitrectomy for stage 4A ROP might reduce the progression to stages 4B and 5 ROP and is therefore the preferred approach, given the improved visual outcome.

What diagnostic imaging test is quantitative for the detection of retinal thickening in diabetic macular edema (DME)?
Correct answer: B. optical coherence tomography
Rationale
DME can be detected by slit-lamp biomicroscopy with contact lens or optical coherence tomography (OCT), but only OCT provides measurements of the thickness of the retina. Fluorescein angiography reveals leakage, which might or might not correspond to thickening. The resolution of B-scan ultrasound is generally too low to reliably detect any increase in macular thickness.

A 65-year-old patient presents with 3-month history of progressive loss of peripheral and central vision, along with photopsias. Fundus examination shows arterial narrowing, and optical coherence tomography shows loss of outer retinal architecture at the level of the photoreceptor outer segments. The electroretinogram (ERG) signal is severely reduced. What is the most appropriate workup for this patient?
Correct answer: A. systemic evaluation for malignancy
Rationale
The loss of retinal function may precede clinical recognition of cancer. Any late-onset, rapidly progressive retinal dysfunction should raise the suspicion that an underlying malignancy is causing an autoimmune retinopathy. Thromboembolic of infectious etiology is unlikely to present with progressive vision loss over months. Inherited retinal diseases usually manifest early in life.

Under what condition is laser photocoagulation an acceptable treatment for choroidal neovascularization (CNV)?
Correct answer: D. extrafoveal choroidal neovascular membrane
Rationale
Laser photocoagulation is no longer the first-line treatment for exudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD). It is also not recommended for myopic neovascularization, due to concerns for laser scar expansion into the central macula.
Extrafoveal choroidal neovascular membrane may be treated with laser photocoagulation if the treating physician believes there is minimal risk of scar expansion into the fovea.

Q3546

A 12-year-old boy is hit in the eye with a baseball. Weeks later, following resolution of the submacular hemorrhage, the finding shown in the photo is noted. The patient's visual acuity is 20/30. What is the most appropriate initial management?
Correct answer: C. observation
Rationale
This clinical scenario alludes to a traumatic choroidal rupture. Traumatic choroidal ruptures occur when the eye is compressed along its anterior-posterior axis, which disrupts the relatively inelastic Bruch membrane. While choroidal neovascularization is a late complication possible with choroidal rupture, which would be treated with an anti-VEGF agent, at this time there is no clinical evidence of this pathology and the patient has good vision. The most appropriate management at this time is observation.

Q3547

A 24-year-old woman presents with acute onset, paracentral “flashing lights” in 1 eye, nasal visual field loss by confrontation in both eyes, and normal visual acuity in both eyes. Vitreous cells are present posteriorly in both eyes. The fundus is otherwise unremarkable. Visual field, multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG), and optical coherence tomography (OCT) testing reveal scotomas corresponding to focally decreased mfERG responses and outer retinal layer disruption in both eyes. What is this patient’s most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. acute zonal occult outer retinopathy
Rationale
The findings are most consistent with acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR). This idiopathic condition typically affects young women with myopia. The acute onset of posterior photopsias is common to many posterior inflammatory conditions, including multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) and multifocal choroiditis; however, the early disruption of outer retina on optical coherence tomography (OCT) differentiates AZOOR from both MEWDS or multifocal choroiditis. Acute macular neuroretinopathy is characterized by 1 or multiple brick-colored wedge-shaped or slightly elevated lesions adjacent to or near the fovea, as well as transitory reduction of the visual acuity in affected eyes. Intermediate uveitis is characterized by anterior vitreous cells. Further, MEWDS is characterized by multiple small gray, white, or yellow-white dots at the level of the outer retina and typically presents unilaterally.

Q3548

An eye with a penetrating injury has a corneal laceration. What would be an indication to perform an immediate vitrectomy in addition to the immediate primary wound repair?
Correct answer: C. intravitreal foreign body
Rationale
An eye with a penetrating injury should undergo microsurgical repair, in which incarcerated uvea is repositioned or excised, as soon as possible. Immediate vitrectomy may be necessary if a retained intravitreal foreign body is suspected.
Posterior extension of a laceration requires exploration and primary wound closure, if possible. Vitreous hemorrhage and uveal prolapse are not indications for an immediate vitrectomy.

Q3549
Retina & Vitreous
What noninvasive diagnostic test is most specific for detecting retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell death?
Correct answer: C. fundus autofluorescence (FAF)
Rationale
Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) is a rapid, noncontact, noninvasive way to image fluorophores in the ocular fundus. Excitation light is introduced to the eye, and fluorescence from intrinsic fluorophores is detected by excluding the imaging of that excitation light via the use of a barrier filter. The main source of autofluorescence from the fundus is lipofuscin in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). If an RPE cell dies, its contained lipofuscin goes away, resulting in a loss of autofluorescence. These areas appear dark in autofluorescence images. This principle can be used to monitor the absence of RPE cells in geographic atrophy, a manifestation of nonexudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Fundus photography is not specific for detecting RPE cell death. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a noninvasive, noncontact imaging modality that produces micrometer-resolution images of tissue. While OCT may show areas consistent with RPE scarring and/or death, it is not as specific to RPE health as fundus autofluoresence.

Q3550
Retina & Vitreous
Following fluorescein angiography, what additional care is appropriate?
Correct answer: A. Observe the patient for signs of delayed adverse reactions.
Rationale
Most patients tolerate fluorescein angiography well without adverse effects or sequelae. Simple observation of the patient for several minutes after completion of the test is sufficient to detect an allergic reaction. Diphenhydramine, not aspirin, is most commonly used if mild signs of allergy appear. Avoidance of sunlight is not necessary because, unlike for verteporfin, no increased sun sensitivity results from fluorescein administration. A color change in the urine is expected as the dye exits the body and does not suggest an infection.

When atrophy develops in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), what other tissue also undergoes atrophy?
Correct answer: B. choriocapillaris
Rationale
Atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) frequently results in adjacent outer segment and choriocapillaris atrophy. These 3 layers are interdependent on each other. The remaining retinal and outer choroidal layers are not affected by RPE loss.

Q3552

What is a characteristic clinical finding suggestive of hypertensive choroidopathy?
Correct answer: D. linear streaks of hyperpigmentation
Rationale
In hypertensive choroidopathy, lobular nonperfusion of the choriocapillaris can occur, resulting in Elschnig spots (hyperpigmented spots surrounded by margins of hypopigmentation [see Figure]) or Siegrist streaks (linear configurations of hyperpigmentation following the meridional course of choroidal arteries). Sub–internal limiting membrane hemorrhages, retinal neovascularization, and cystoid macular edema (CME) are characteristic sequelae of hypertensive retinopathy, not hypertensive choroidopathy.

Q3553

Sclopetaria is most commonly related to what kinds of injuries?
Correct answer: A. injuries from paintballs and firearms
Rationale
Sclopetaria, or traumatic choroidal disruption, results from high-speed projectile injuries to the globe, such as from paintballs and firearms. It manifests with choroidal and retinal rupture and necrosis with associated hemorrhage. Chorioretinal scarring follows the acute process. Retinal detachment is rare.

Q3554
Retina & Vitreous
For a patient with diabetic retinopathy, what is an indication for panretinal (peripheral scatter) photocoagulation?
Correct answer: B. moderate neovascularization of the disc and vitreous hemorrhage
Rationale
Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) is the mainstay of treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). The treatment indications are still largely based on findings in the Diabetic Retinopathy Study (DRS) (Clinical Trial 5-4), a pivotal clinical trial. For patients with high-risk PDR, treatment with PRP is almost always recommended. The goal of PRP is regression or involution of neovascularization. PRP destroys ischemic retina and increases oxygen tension in the eye. High-risk PDR was defined in the DRS as having any 1 of the following findings:
  • mild neovascularization of the disc (NVD) with vitreous hemorrhage
  • moderate to severe NVD with or without vitreous hemorrhage (≥DRS standard 10A, showing one-fourth to one-third disc area of NVD)
  • moderate (one-half disc area) neovascularization elsewhere (NVE) with vitreous hemorrhage
OR any 3 of the 4 following findings:
  • vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage
  • new vessels
  • new vessels located on or near the optic disc
  • moderate to severe extent of new vessels
Moderate neovascularization of the disc and vitreous hemorrhage represents high-risk PDR and, therefore, requires PRP. Venous beading in 2 quadrants and intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms in 4 quadrants meet criteria for severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy. Severe NPDR is defined as having any 1 of the following features:
  • severe intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms in 4 quadrants
  • venous beading in 2 or more quadrants
  • intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs) in 1 or more quadrants
Severe NPDR was found to have a 15% chance of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year. Very severe NPDR, defined as having 2 or more of these features, increased the chance of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year to 45%. Patients with severe NPDR or worse should be considered for early treatment with panretinal photocoagulation. Nerve fiber layer infarcts are an indication of ischemia, but represent a reduction of retinal tissue analogous to retinal laser tissue necrosis. They are not an indication for PRP.

Q3555
Retina & Vitreous
What is the zoonotic vector of West Nile Virus?
Correct answer: A. mosquitoes
Rationale
West Nile viral retinopathy is caused by a single-stranded flavivirus that is transmitted to humans by mosquitoes of the genus Culex. Ocular manifestations typically occur in very ill diabetic patients with encephalitis. The characteristic lesions are bilateral multifocal chorioretinitis that includes distinctive curvilinear clusters that often run parallel to the direction of the nerve fiber layer.

What is the middle layer of the Bruch membrane composed of?
Correct answer: D. elastic fibers
Rationale
The Bruch membrane has 5 layers. Starting with the innermost, these layers are the basement membrane of RPE, the inner collagenous zone, the middle layer of elastic fibers, the outer collagenous zone, and the basement membrane of the endothelium of the choriocapillaris.

What paraneoplastic retinal degeneration is associated with antirecoverin antibodies?
Correct answer: D. cancer-associated retinopathy
Rationale
Antirecoverin antibodies might be found in the serum of patients with cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) and are highly suggestive of the presence of a systemic malignancy, such as small cell carcinoma of the lung. In some cases, these systemic malignancies might not be clinically detectable for some time after the onset of vision loss. Other antiretinal antibodies that can be present in patients with retinal degeneration include antienolase and antitransducin antibodies; because they are less specific, their presence supports a diagnosis of CAR less strongly. In such cases, autoimmune retinopathy is the preferred diagnostic terminology.

Q3558

A patient with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes presents with vision loss (20/200) in 1 eye. Clinical examination shows mild inferior vitreous hemorrhage, minimal macular edema outside of the central macula, and a well-perfused optic nerve. Fluorescein angiography demonstrates an area of neovascularization elsewhere and a foveal avascular zone (FAZ) of 1500 microns. What is the most likely cause of poor vision?
Correct answer: B. ischemic maculopathy
Rationale
Vision loss in patients with diabetic retinopathy can be associated with the abnormalities that include capillary leakage, ischemic maculopathy (capillary occlusion), and sequelae from ischemia-induced neovascularization. Vitreous hemorrhage, macular edema, tractional detachment, and macular ischemia can all cause vision loss. In the above vignette, macular ischemia (FAZ ~1500 microns) is the most likely cause, since the vitreous hemorrhage is outside of the visual axis (inferior) and the macular edema is noncentral.

Q3559

A 12-year-old child presents with blurry vision. His fundus photo is shown in Fig 1. The rest of the ocular examination of this eye and the other eye are normal. Blood work shows eosinophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. toxocariasis
Rationale
Toxocariasis is unilateral in most cases and typically has 1 of 3 presentations: (1) a peripheral granuloma, which often produces a traction band that extends toward the macula and occasionally mimics unilateral intermediate uveitis with snowbank formation; (2) a posterior pole granuloma, which can decrease vision dramatically when the central macula is involved; or (3) a moderate to severe panuveitis that can mimic endogenous endophthalmitis.
Toxoplasmosis produces an area of chorioretinitis adjacent to an old scar. Coats disease can produce subretinal exudation, but the pathology is usually localized to the peripheral intraretinal vasculature. Best disease is associated with bilateral vitelliform lesions.

Q3560
Retina & Vitreous
What disorder can be associated with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas?
Correct answer: C. pheochromocytoma
Rationale
Von Hippel–Lindau disease is characterized by retinal capillary hemangioblastomas in association with angiomatous lesions of the central nervous system and cysts and tumors in the viscera. Manifestations include cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pancreatic cysts, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma. Diffuse choroidal hemangioma is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome, whereas circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas have no systemic disease or syndrome association. Retinal astrocytic hamartomas, or retinal astrocytomas, are benign lesions and may be associated with tuberous sclerosis or neurofibromatosis type 1. On the other hand, central nervous system astrocytomas can be malignant tumors. Retinal arterial macroaneurysms are associated with idiopathic systemic hypertension and atherosclerotic disease.

What is the mode of inheritance of the disease pictured here?
Correct answer: B. autosomal dominant
Rationale
The photo shown is the characteristic "yolk" stage of Best disease or Best vitelliform dystrophy, during which visual acuity is typically good. Best disease is an autosomal dominant maculopathy caused by mutations in the Best1 (VMD2) gene. The encoded protein bestrophin localizes to the basolateral plasma membrane of the RPE and functions as a transmembrane ion channel.

Q3562

In normal ocular development, vascularization of the temporal retina is completed by what gestational age?
Correct answer: B. 40 weeks
Rationale
Normally, retinal vascular development begins during week 16 of gestation. Mesenchymal tissue containing spindle cells is the source of retinal vessels. Typically, retinal vascular development is complete by 40 weeks of gestation. Thus, infants who are born at a gestational age of 30 weeks or less are at a higher risk of developing retinopathy of prematurity.

Q3563
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common systemic condition associated with the findings shown in the figure?
Correct answer: B. pseudoxanthoma elasticum
Rationale
Angioid streaks have been associated with a number of systemic disorders and with aging. The most common systemic association is with pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ABCC6 gene. PXE results in calcification and other mineralization of elastin, most visibly as yellow papules in the flexor regions of the skin ("plucked chicken skin"). PXE affects approximately 1 in 50,000 people worldwide. Other systemic disorders associated with angioid streaks include Paget disease of bone, beta thalassemia, sickle cell disease, and Ehlers-Danlos disease. Angioid streaks are typically more prominent adjacent to or can extend from the optic disc, in contrast to Bruch membrane ruptures from trauma or high myopia ("lacquer cracks").
Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease are associated with uveitis but not angioid streaks.
Oculocutaneous albinism can have depigmented skin spots, but not papules. Angioid streaks are not a feature of ocular cutaneous albinism. Angioid streaks can be associated with numerous systemic diseases, the most common being pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE), also known as Groenblad-Strandberg syndrome. A popular mnemonic used to recall the more common associations is PEPSI: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Ehler-Danlos syndrome, Paget disease of bone, Sickle cell disease and other hemoglobinopathies, Idiopathic.
Other systemic associations include abetalipoproteinemia, acromegaly, diabetes mellitus, facial angiomatosis, hemochromatosis, hemolytic anemia, hereditary spherocytosis, hypercalcinosis, hyperphosphatemia, lead poisoning, myopia, neurofibromatosis, senile elastosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis.

Q3564

Surgical exploration may be done for evaluation of suspected scleral rupture following blunt ocular trauma. In what location are occult ruptures often found?
Correct answer: B. posterior to the insertion of a rectus muscle
Rationale
Occult scleral rupture after blunt trauma is often found posterior to the insertion of a rectus muscle, since this is an area where sclera is naturally thin. The sclera is thicker at the equator, fovea, and anterior to the rectus insertion, making these areas less likely to rupture during blunt trauma.
The 2 most important locations to inspect are: 1) at the limbus and 2) under the rectus muscle insertions.

Q3565
Retina & Vitreous
What electrophysiologic test is most useful in detecting primary ganglion cell disease?
Correct answer: D. pattern electroretinogram (ERG)
Rationale
The pattern ERG is the electrophysiologic test most useful in detecting primary ganglion cell disease. The multifocal ERG can determine objectively whether macular dysfunction is present, for example, in the early detection of hydroxychloroquine toxicity. The photopic full field ERG indicates cone dysfunction outside the macula, facilitating the distinction between a macular dystrophy (normal ERG) and a cone or cone–rod dystrophy. The electro-oculogram  assesses the health of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), as well as the interaction between the RPE and the photoreceptors, by measuring the changes in the corneoretinal standing potential that occur during scotopic or photopic adaptation. The principal use of the EOG in clinical practice is in the diagnosis of Best vitelliform macular dystrophy.

Q3566

What effect does demyelinating optic neuritis with recovered visual acuity have on pattern-reversal visual evoked potential (VEP) testing?
Correct answer: D. delayed pattern-reversal VEP
Rationale
Optic nerve disease often results in peak-time delay in the pattern-reversal visual evoked potential (VEP). The predominant abnormality in nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is amplitude reduction rather than peak-time delay. Delayed pattern-reversal VEPs are frequently present in macular dysfunction. Demyelinating optic neuritis is almost invariably associated with continuing peak-time delay even after recovery of visual acuity. Compared with pattern-reversal VEPs, pattern-appearance VEPs are relatively insensitive to the presence of nystagmus.

A 19-year-old man is struck in the left eye with a paintball. Visual acuity is 20/200 OS. Examination shows no afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure is 18. There is no subconjunctival hemorrhage. The anterior chamber is formed. Fundus examination shows thickened opaque retinal whitening in the macula. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
Correct answer: B. observation
Rationale
The clinical presentation described is consistent with commotio retinae. The appropriate management for commotio retinae is observation.
High-dose intravenous steroids have no role in management of commotio retinae. 
Anterior chamber paracentesis can be used in cases of acute retinal artery occlusion but has no role in commotio retinae.
Laser photocoagulation can be used for a retinal break but is not used for commotio retinae.

Q3568
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common ocular vascular complication associated with hypertensive retinopathy?
Correct answer: A. retinal venous occlusion
Rationale
The most common ocular complication of hypertension, other than hypertensive retinopathy, is a retinal vein occlusion. Systemic hypertension is a risk factor for branch retinal vein occlusions (BRVOs), central retinal vein occlusions (CRVOs), and hemicentral retinal vein occlusions. In addition, systemic hypertension is a risk factor for nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy, but not arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. Iris neovascularization is a late complication of central and hemicentral retinal vein occlusion and can occur in up to 10% of cases of CRVO; systemic hypertension is not a direct (but indirect) risk factor. Idiopathic retinal macroaneurysms are associated with hypertension but are much rarer than vein occlusions.

Peripheral retinal excavations are a risk factor for what disorder?
Correct answer: A. retinal detachment
Rationale
Tears may occur at the site of peripheral retinal excavations, which in turn may lead to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Peripheral retinal excavations may represent a mild form of lattice degeneration, with associated firm vitreoretinal adhesions. They are often aligned with meridional folds. These lesions have no known association with retinoschisis, peripheral cystic degeneration, or cobblestone degeneration.

A 10-year-old child presents with decreased vision in both eyes, photophobia, and decreased color vision. Fluorescein angiography reveals a dark choroid in both eyes. A mutation in what gene is most commonly associated with this disease?
Correct answer: C. ABCA4
Rationale
ABCA4

Stargardt disease is a hereditary retinal dystrophy most commonly associated with an autosomal recessive mutation in the ABCA4 gene. Mutations in ABCA4 are also associated with cone-rod dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa. Autosomal dominant mutations in genes such as PRPH2 can result in Stargardt disease but are less common. Autosomal recessive Leber congenital amaurosis and retinitis pigmentosa can be due to mutations in RPE65. Mutations in BEST1 are associated with Best disease and retinitis pigmentosa.

Q3571

An ophthalmologist is surgically exploring a blunt globe injury secondary to a racquetball trauma. The injury presented with 360 degrees of hemorrhagic chemosis and an intraocular pressure of 3 mm Hg. Intraoperatively, a complete 360 peritomy is performed, with no identification of globe rupture. What is the next most appropriate course of action?
Correct answer: C. exploration under the rectus muscles
Rationale
Severe blunt trauma can cause scleral rupture. The most common sites of scleral rupture are at the limbus and parallel to and underneath rectus muscle insertions at anatomic areas of thinning. Scleral rupture is associated with markedly decreased ocular ductions, boggy conjunctival chemosis, deep anterior chamber, severe vitreous hemorrhage, and usually hypotony, although intraocular pressure may also be normal or elevated. In this case, suspicion of occult scleral rupture is high, warranting further exploration, with disinsertion of one of more rectus muscles in order to identify the rupture site. Scleral lacerations or ruptures are typically closed with  7-0, 8-0, or 9-0 nonabsorbable suture. Some specialists recommend prophylactic vitrectomy and/or placement of a scleral buckle at the time of primary repair of some perforating ocular injuries, but the primary goal of most open globe repairs is to achieve corneoscleral wound closure.

Systemic hypertension represents the most common risk factor for the development of a BRVO. The other conditions listed (hepatic insufficiency, diabetes insipidus, and hypothyroidism) have not been shown to represent risk factors for BRVO. Additional risk factors for BRVO include cardiovascular disease, hyperlipidemia, and glaucoma.

An ophthalmologist examines the optical coherence tomography (OCT) image from a 56-year-old diabetic patient with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. The patient has blurred vision in the eye illustrated by the figure. What condition is most likely the cause for this patient's visual reduction?
Correct answer: B. cystoid macular edema
Rationale
This patient has cystic spaces and thickening on OCT that supports the diagnosis of diabetic macular edema. Because of the topographic location of the retinal thickening and cysts, diabetic macular edema is the most likely explanation for their visual decline.
Although epiretinal membranes (ERMs) are often seen in nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, there does not appear to be contraction or antero-posterior traction at the edges of the ERM in this OCT image. Exudative macular degeneration could cause retinal edema, but would likely show subretinal thickening or other subretinal abnormality on the OCT. In vitreomacular traction (VMT) syndrome, the posterior hyaloid remains tethered at the macula, usually at the fovea, causing tractional foveal distortion, cystic edema, and in severe cases tractional foveal detachment. OCT is useful to demonstrate the vitreoretinal interface abnormalities and the tractional effects of VMT syndrome on the foveal architecture. While this OCT shows cystic edema, there is no traction visible.

What is 1 of the 3 criteria needed to meet the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) definition of clinically significant diabetic macular edema (CSME)?
Correct answer: B. Retinal thickening is greater than 1 disc diameter in extent, within 1 disc diameter of the macular center.
Rationale
The definition of CSME includes 1, 2, or all of the following findings:
  • Retinal thickening within 500 µm of the macular center
  • Hard exudates within 500 µm of the macular center, with adjacent retinal thickening
  • One or more disc diameters of retinal thickening, part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the macular center

In randomized clinical trials evaluating therapy for branch retinal vein occlusions, for what indication is intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy management proven effective?
Correct answer: A. macular edema
Rationale
Although anti-VEGF has been demonstrated to cause regression of retinal neovascularization in diabetes and iris neovascularization in central retinal vein occlusion, no study has confirmed these effects in the setting of branch retinal vein occlusions. However, macular edema, the most common vision-threatening complication of branch retinal vein occlusion, has been shown to be reduced during treatment with anti-VEGF. It is unknown whether use of anti-VEGF results in macular edema-associated or resultant retinal damage if it is later discontinued.

What bacteria commonly causes endogenous endophthalmitis in patients with liver abscesses?
Correct answer: D. Klebsiella species
Rationale
Klebsiella species

A wide range of bacteria can cause endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis. In North America, 40% of cases occur in patients with endocarditis, most typically caused by either Staphylococcus or Streptococcus species. In contrast, 60% of endogenous endophthalmitis cases in Asia occur in patients with liver abscesses caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Nearly one-third of cases occur in patients who have urinary tract infections, most often caused by Escherichia coli. Other cases can be associated with intravenous drug use or with procedures known to produce bacteremia, particularly placement of indwelling catheters.

What circumstance represents a definite indication to treat an atrophic retinal hole?
Correct answer: A. association with symptomatic retinal detachment
Rationale
Atrophic holes in an eye with retinal detachment should be treated to successfully treat the retinal detachment (see table).
Atrophic holes are generally not associated with vitreoretinal traction and have a low risk of retinal detachment. For this reason, atrophic holes do not always have to be treated, even if they are associated with lattice degeneration or present in a patient with high myopia or with a previous history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye, although these are softer indications to consider prophylactic treatment.

A 24-year-old man felt something strike his right eye after hammering a metal pipe at work. Examination reveals a shallow anterior chamber, cataract, and vitreous hemorrhage. What is the most appropriate ancillary test to further evaluate this patient's injury?
Correct answer: D. computed tomography
Rationale
Computed tomography is the most appropriate test in cases with a suspected intraocular foreign body. Imaging can be obtained quickly and has high sensitivity in detecting the foreign body.
Magnetic resonance imaging is contraindicated in cases with a suspected intraocular foreign body, because metallic foreign bodies may move under the magnetic field, causing further injury.
B-scan echography can be used to detect an intraocular foreign body; however, it is not the most appropriate test in the described clinical vignette, and must be used with care to avoid causing ocular compression when a ruptured globe is present.
Fluorescein angiography is not indicated in cases with a suspected intraocular foreign body.

Q3588
