A 22-year-old man presents with night blindness, constricted visual fields, posterior subcapsular cataracts, and cystoid macular edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. retinitis pigmentosa
Rationale
This constellation of features is characteristic for retinitis pigmentosa (RP), a heterogeneous group of degenerative retinal disorders that lead to progressive loss of visual function. Affected patients generally complain of night blindness (nyctalopia) and midperipheral scotomas ("ring scotomas") or constriction of their visual fields. Clinical signs of RP include the narrowing of retinal vessels, bone spicule pigmentation within the retina, and waxy pallor of the optic nerve. Some patients may also develop cystoid macular edema and posterior subcapsular cataract.
Cone dystrophy is characterized by the progressive loss of visual acuity, poor color discrimination, and development of a central scotoma. In advanced cases, there may be a localized bilateral macular bull's-eye atrophy pattern or a more diffuse appearance. Vitamin A deficiency and cancer-associated retinopathy present with poor scotopic acuity, constricted visual fields, and variable electroretinogram b-wave amplitude reduction. However, cystoid macular edema and subcapsular cataract are not features associated with either of these conditions.

A 19-year-old deaf patient with a known pigmentary retinopathy presents for ptosis repair. His ocular motility is impaired. For what cardiovascular disorder should he be evaluated?

Rationale
This patient presents with the constellation of signs of Kearns-Sayre syndrome. This syndrome consists of features of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) plus pigmentary retinopathy. CPEO is associated with heart block, and placement of a cardiac pacemaker may be life-saving. Other features include upgaze limitation, decreased levator function, increased cerebrospinal fluid protein, deafness, vestibular dysfunction, and mitochondrial myopathy with fibers on muscle biopsy. Marfan syndrome is associated with aortic aneurysm and ectopia lentis, but not a pigmentary retinopathy, deafness, or ptosis. Carotid dissection can be traumatic or spontaneous but has no association with CPEO. Congestive heart failure is not associated with CPEO.

The Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion Study (BVOS) predated the use of intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy or intravitreal steroids. All eyes were observed for at least 3 months to permit the maximum spontaneous resolution of the edema and intraretinal blood.

Rationale
The fundus photograph shows a superotemporal branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO).
Essential hypertension is an important risk factor for development of BRVO. Diabetes insipidus, radiation exposure, and renal insufficiency are not associated with BRVO.

Q3594
Retina & Vitreous
A healthy 45-year-old woman complains of worsening central vision over the past year. Fundus examination demonstrates symmetric changes as depicted in this image bilaterally.  Fluorescein angiography demonstrates a dark choroid. What test is most appropriate to establish a definitive diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. genetic testing
Rationale
Stargardt disease is an autosomal recessive macular dystrophy caused by mutations in the ABCA4 gene. Patients may present with central vision complaints as early as childhood and as late as age 50, with highly variable phenotypic manifestations. The differential diagnosis includes age-related macular degeneration and hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine retinal toxicity.
A definitive diagnosis can be established by genetic testing. The classic finding of a “silent choroid” on fluorescein angiography is not always present, and the electroretinogram is typically normal. The findings on fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography (OCT) can exhibit features that overlap with other macular diseases.

Q3595
Retina & Vitreous
A 35-year-old man who has been followed by an ophthalmologist for retinitis pigmentosa recently experienced blurred vision. Last year his vision was 20/20 OU, but on examination now his visual acuity is 20/40 OD and 20/20 OS. What is the most likely cause of his central visual loss?
Correct answer: C. cystoid macular edema
Rationale
In this case of asymmetric mild vision loss in RP from 20/20 to 20/40, the most likely cause is cystoid macular edema. Alternatives include development of a posterior subcapsular cataract or advanced constriction of the midperipheral and peripheral loss. Secondary glaucoma only has a weak association with RP and would not be responsible for a mild decrease in central vision. Cystoid macular edema from RP can be treated with oral acetazaolamide or intravitreal triamcinolone. However, treatment-resistant CME in RP is common.

Q3596
Retina & Vitreous
In a patient with postoperative serous choroidal detachment, what additional feature might an ophthalmologist expect to find?
Correct answer: B. hypotony
Rationale
Postoperative serous choroidal detachments after a glaucoma filtering procedure are generally associated with hypotony. They are more common in myopes than hyperopes, and are painless in contrast to hemorrhagic choroidal detachments, which are typically painful. Most serous choroidal detachments resolve spontaneously or, in rare cases, may require revision of the glaucoma-filtering procedure to reduce hypotony. Rarely will persistent choroidal detachment require surgical drainage. As choroidal detachments are tethered to the sclera at the optic canal and at vortex vein ampullae, the highest point of detachment is typically midway between vortex vein ampullae.

Correct answer: C. individual symptoms and impact on lifestyle
Rationale
The image demonstrates an epiretinal membrane with an associated macular pucker. The patient should be treated based on individual symptoms and the impact of such symptoms on the patient's lifestyle. If the patient is experiencing functional visual impairment, pars plana vitrectomy surgery with epiretinal membrane dissection may be considered. The decision to proceed with surgery should not be based on an arbitrary level of visual acuity, degree of apparent traction, or OCT findings, but these may be useful confirmation if functional visual loss is present.

What test for systemic disease is essential in the workup of a patient with suspected Kearns-Sayre syndrome (retinitis pigmentosa with mitochondrial myopathy)?
Correct answer: D. cardiac conduction defect test
Rationale
Cardiac conduction defects are associated with Kearns-Sayre syndrome (retinitis pigmentosa with mitochondrial myopathy; this syndrome also includes chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia). Audiologic abnormalities are associated with Usher syndrome. While sensorineural hearing loss can occur in Kearns-Sayre syndrome, investigation for cardiac conduction defects is clearly more critical. Fasting serum phytanic acid level abnormalities are associated with Refsum disease. Lipid profile and serum lipoprotein electrophoresis abnormalities are associated with Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome.

Q3599

A small peripapillary vascular lesion is found incidentally during a routine examination on an asymptomatic teenager. Fluorescein angiography documents an arteriovenous malformation without leakage. What is the next step in this patient's management?
Correct answer: C. intracranial and facial imaging
Rationale
Congenital retinal arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) can occur as a feature of Wyburn-Mason syndrome but are more commonly found in isolation. Malformations lack an intervening capillary bed (racemose angioma). Small retinal lesions typically remain asymptomatic and can be observed. A hereditary basis has not been found for Wyburn-Mason syndrome, which can manifest with AVMs of the midbrain, as well as intraosseous AVMs of the maxilla and mandible. Complications can include hemorrhaging during dental procedures. Abdominal imaging is performed in the workup of von Hippel-Lindau disease.

What systemically administered drug can result in a complication of a pigmentary retinopathy?
Correct answer: A. thioridazine

The taxanes (docetaxel, paclitaxel) and niacin can induce a microcystic form of macular edema that is detected on SD-OCT and does not leak on fluorescein angiography. The phenothiazine thioridazine can cause a severe pigmentary retinopathy that can develop within a few weeks or months of high-dose utilization. Toxicity is rare with thioridazine doses of less than 800 mg/day.

Retinal arteriolar macroaneurysms are most commonly associated with systemic hypertension. Complications include macular edema, subretinal hemorrhage, and vitreous hemorrhage. Despite these potential complications, the potential for visual recovery is good.

Serous retinal detachments are differentiated from rhegmatogenous detachments by lacking a retinal break. Additionally, serous retinal detachments will exhibit shifting fluid, depending on the position of the patient's head or eye, as the subretinal fluid is affected by gravitational forces.

MEWDS is characterized by the presence of multiple, small gray-white dots at the level of the deep retina/RPE in the posterior pole. What condition represents the most common indication for scleral buckle surgery?

Rationale
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment represents the most common indication for scleral buckle surgery. This procedure is not indicated for the primary management of choroidal effusion, exudative retinal detachment, or proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Other options for the management of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment include repair by vitrectomy, pneumatic retinopexy, laser demarcation, and, in selected cases, observation.

Retinal vascular sheathing is a common clinical feature of primary idiopathic retinal vasculitis. Subretinal hemorrhage and retinal neovascularization are also not common findings in primary idiopathic retinal vasculitis.

Q3610

On dilated fundus examination, a 41-year-old emmetropic, phakic woman is incidentally found to have an operculated hole. She has no associated lattice degeneration and no prior history of retinal detachment. What is the best treatment option for this patient?
Correct answer: A. observation
Rationale
Asymptomatic flap tears progress to retinal detachment in approximately 5% of cases. Because of this low risk, treatment is not universally recommended in emmetropic, phakic eyes. However, asymptomatic flap tears accompanied by lattice degeneration, myopia, subclinical detachment, aphakia, pseudophakia, or a history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye have an increased risk of retinal detachment, and treatment may be considered. Asymptomatic operculated holes and atrophic holes rarely cause retinal detachment and therefore treatment is not generally recommended.

What is the typical appearance of adult-onset foveomacular dystrophy?
Correct answer: C. bilateral, round or oval, yellow subfoveal lesions
Rationale
Adult-onset foveomacular dystrophy presents as bilateral, round or oval, yellow subfoveal lesions.
Bilateral, butterfly-shaped, yellow macular pigment is seen in butterfly-type pattern dystrophy.
Fishnet pattern of yellow-orange or brown pigment is seen in reticular dystrophy.
Coarse pigment mottling in central macula is seen in fundus pulverulentus.

Q3612
Retina & Vitreous
A 23-year-old athletic male complains of decreased vision in the upper visual field of his left eye. Examination reveals a retinal dialysis from 4 to 6:30 o'clock associated with a shallow inferior retinal detachment just posterior to the equator. What is the preferred treatment?
Correct answer: A. Schedule a scleral buckle procedure for the next available time.
Rationale
Retinal dialyses are notorious for delayed presentation of associated retinal detachments. Because this patient’s detachment is inferior and distant from the macula, the urgency of this situation is moderated. Retinal detachments associated with retinal dialyses have very high reattachment rates with scleral buckle procedures. When performed in the absence of a pars plana vitrectomy, scleral buckle procedures utilize retinal cryopexy to create chorioretinal adhesions around any retinal breaks, with or without external drainage of subretinal fluid. This approach has the advantage of avoiding the need for a gas bubble which would promote cataractogenesis in this young phakic patient.
In the event that vitrectomy, laser, and gas injection were considered, a shorter duration gas such as SF6 would be preferred, to avoid prolonged need for eye down positioning. Vitrectomy is the preferred surgical option, over scleral buckle with retinal cryopexy, in cases with giant retinal tears, proliferative vitreoretinopathy, poorly defined breaks, or pseudophakic patients in whom it is uncertain that all breaks have been identified. Observation of a symptomatic retinal detachment is contraindicated.

Q3613
Retina & Vitreous
A patient presents with a suspected open-globe injury from a construction accident. The patient is unsure what hit his eye. Vision from the eye is light perception only. External examination reveals a total hyphema and 360 degrees of subconjunctival hemorrhage. The patient has not had anything to eat or drink in at least 8 hours. What is the best next step in management?
Correct answer: C. computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain and orbits
Rationale
The first step in a suspected open-globe injury should be a CT scan of the brain and orbits. A CT scan will evaluate the shape of the globe and help identify an intraocular foreign body (IOFB). Additionally, it can identify other head and facial trauma. MRI is helpful for identifying wood or glass foreign bodies that may be difficult to detect on CT. However, if a metallic foreign body is suspected, as in this case in a construction accident, MRI should be avoided, because movement of a metallic IOFB could cause additional damage. Although immediate globe exploration in the operating room can be performed, it is inferior to CT scan and risks causing extrusion of ocular contents. While this patient will almost certainly need surgery, imaging should be performed first, as the findings may impact the surgical plan.

Q3614
Retina & Vitreous
In an eye with retinoschisis, what examination findings are associated with an increased risk of progression to retinal detachment?
Correct answer: D. inner and outer layer breaks
Rationale
The presence of inner and outer layer breaks in retinoschisis is associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment. However, the presence of outer layer breaks (but not inner breaks) can lead to a localized retinal detachment that usually does not progress and seldom requires treatment. The presence of a bullous inner layer does not predispose to retinal detachment. Finally, the presence of a demarcation line in an eye with retinoschisis indicates that a chronic localized retinal detachment is present or has spontaneously regressed; this is not likely to lead to a progressive retinal detachment.

Q3615

A 40-year-old man presents with an active focal retinochoroiditis with an adjacent retinochoroidal scar. The patient recalls no prior episodes of uveitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. acquired toxoplasmosis reactivation
Rationale
The vast majority of ocular toxoplasmosis is acquired. The presence of a retinochoroidal scar is strong support for prior infection, meaning that this particular episode is not primary and that infection could have occurred either at or long after birth. The absence of an adjacent or nearby retinochoroidal scar together with a positive serum test result for anti-Toxoplasma gondii IgM antibody would constitute strong supportive evidence for an acutely acquired infection. Cytomegalovirus retinitis is rare and is typically observed in severely immunosuppressed individuals.

Q3616

For this asymptomatic, 35-year-old man with a corrected visual acuity of 20/20 OU and the fundus shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. familial dominant drusen
Rationale
The image demonstrates macular drusen. In an asymptomatic 35-year-old patient, the most likely diagnosis is familial dominant drusen, which could be confirmed by examination of first-degree relatives. Other less likely diagnoses would include cuticular drusen (basal laminar drusen), Sorsby macular dystrophy, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type 2, or malattia leventinese (radial drusen, Doyne macular dystrophy, or mutation in EFEMP1). A minimum age cutoff of 50 years is usually used to differentiate age-related macular degeneration from the earlier presenting phenotypes. Adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy (pattern dystrophy) is characterized by the presence of more discrete, localized macular lesions unlike the diffuse drusen demonstrated in the image. The flecks associated with Stargardt disease tend to be less diffuse than familial dominant drusen. In addition, a 35-year-old patient with Stargardt disease would, in general, have a reduction in visual acuity.

For the condition illustrated, what is the most common associated systemic condition?

The image demonstrates retinitis and retinal hemorrhage from cytomegalovirus. This condition is most commonly associated with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. It can also result from immune suppression caused by chemotherapy or as required for organ transplantation. Antiviral therapy, typically with oral valganciclovir, is indicated for the treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis. If HIV is found, additional systemic highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) should be initiated.

This patient is presenting with a macular hole. For the majority of patients with macular hole, the cause is unknown or idiopathic. For the remainder of patients, myopia and direct blunt ocular trauma are associated characteristics. Q3619
Retina & Vitreous
What fluorescein angiographic feature would be seen in a patient with an episode of acute, severe hypertension who eventually develops the lesions shown in the figure?
Correct answer: D. early choroidal hypoperfusion followed by multiple subretinal areas of leakage in the late phases
Rationale
Hypertension may lead to hypertensive retinopathy, choroidopathy, and/or optic neuropathy. The image shows Elschnig spots, which develop from lobular nonperfusion of the choriocapillaris that eventually becomes hyperpigmented and surrounded by margins of hypopigmentation, indicating hypertensive choroidopathy.
Choroidal involvement includes fluorescein angiographic findings of early-phase focal choroidal hypoperfusion and late multiple subretinal areas of leakage. Progressive irregular hyperfluorescence at the level of the RPE occurs in acute idiopathic maculopathy. Collateral vessels have a larger caliber and do not leak on fluorescein angiography (FA). In branch retinal vein occlusion, these must be distinguished from neovascularization. Areas of retinal capillary nonperfusion are characteristic of ischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO).

What is the appropriate management of an asymptomatic patient with lattice degeneration without breaks?
Correct answer: A. a discussion of the warning signs of retinal detachment
Rationale
Lattice degeneration without any breaks can be safely observed; however, the patient should be made aware of the need for prompt evaluation if there are signs or symptoms of retinal tear or retinal detachment.
Prophylactic laser or scleral buckle is not required in an asymptomatic patient with lattice degeneration. These patients can be followed with annual examinations.

Q3621
Retina & Vitreous
What feature of the choroid mitigates the potential thermal damage associated with light absorption?
Correct answer: D. rapid blood flow
Rationale
The high speed of blood flow through the choroid helps to dissipate thermal energy from light absorption in addition to maintaining the oxygen needs of the photoreceptors (and resulting in high oxygen tension in venous blood). The multilayer arterial structure of the choroid, which is thicker centrally than peripherally, allows blood to be delivered across the extent of the retina, with an accompanying decrease in pressure before reaching the choriocapillaris.

In a premature infant born at 29 weeks’ gestation, what is the appropriate time for the initial screening examination for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?
Correct answer: D. 4–6 weeks  after birth
Rationale
Screening should be done on all infants with a birth weight of less than 1500 g or a gestational age of 30 weeks or less. The first examination should generally be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of postnatal age or, alternatively, between 31 and 33 weeks’ postconceptional or postmenstrual age, whichever is later. In this case the infant is born at 29 weeks, hence the first examination should be done 4 to 6 weeks after birth.

Q3623
Retina & Vitreous
A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows a well-circumscribed intraconal mass with uniform enhancement indenting the posterior globe. What funduscopic finding is expected?
Correct answer: C. choroidal folds
Rationale
An intraconal mass can cause pressure on the posterior globe, leading to choroidal folds. Another cause of choroidal folds from external forces is thyroid eye disease. Other causes of choroidal folds include posterior scleritis, choroidal infiltration from lymphoma, hypotony, and a poorly characterized condition in which middle-aged adults develop symmetric choroidal folds bilaterally. Localized choroidal folds can be seen in association with choroidal neovascularization, choroidal neoplasms, and scleral buckles.

Patton lines are fine folds that course circumferentially around the optic nerve head in the setting of increased intracranial pressure. Papilledema is optic nerve swelling secondary to increased intracranial pressure, which would not be expected from an intraconal mass. Choroidal thickness is inversely related to degree of myopia and increasing age; subretinal drusenoid deposits also increase the risk of geographic atrophy. Choroidal atrophy would not be expected to occur secondary to an orbital mass.

Q3624

A 19-year-old man developed an acute reduction in central vision, a central scotoma, and a yellow spot in his central macula. What drug may lead to this presentation?
Correct answer: B. alkyl nitrites
Rationale
“Poppers” is a slang term for alkyl nitrites, which are a class of chemical used as recreational drugs. The chemicals are inhaled to induce euphoria and relax smooth muscles, usually in preparation for sexual activity. In rare cases, use can lead to acute central scotoma and vision reduction associated with a yellow, “vitelliform”-like macular lesion. In rare cases, MEK inhibitors, which are a class of chemotherapeutic agents, and sildenafil have been associated with serous macular fluid, which may simulate central serous choroidopathy. Corticosteroids may precipitate serous exudation from central serous retinopathy.

A law student presents to the emergency department for evaluation of “blurry vision,” and is noted to have bilateral serous retinal detachments with whitish dots underneath the retinal surface on examination. The most likely diagnosis in this scenario has been associated with use of what class of medication?
Correct answer: D. corticosteroids
Rationale
The most likely diagnosis in this case, suggested by bilateral serous retinal detachments with "white dots" under the retina, is central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC), which has been associated with corticosteroid use. Patients may present with blurred or dim vision, micropsia, or metamorphopsia and may have highly preserved visual acuity that typically improves with hyperopic correction. The white dots visualized are theorized to represent macrophages with phagocytized outer segments. SSRIs, beta blockers, and calcium channel blockers have not been associated with CSC.

What is an indication for prompt surgical intervention in the setting of a visually significant vitreous hemorrhage secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy?

Poor visual acuity in the fellow eye of a patient with a visually significant vitreous hemorrhage secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy represents an indication for prompt surgical intervention to allow for visual rehabilitation. An extramacular traction retinal detachment may remain stable and does not represent an indication for prompt intervention. Other indications for prompt vitrectomy would include bilateral vitreous hemorrhage, ultrasound evidence of a retinal tear or rhegmatogenous detachment, or tractional retinal detachment that threatens the macula.

What represents the most common mechanism of traumatic avulsion of the optic nerve?

Sudden increase in IOP, causing rupture of the lamina cribrosa, represents the most common mechanism of traumatic avulsion of the optic nerve. Extreme rotation and/or forward displacement of the globe, and penetrating orbital injury causing a rearward pull on the optic nerve, are other potential mechanisms. Penetrating globe injury, causing a sudden decompression injury, is not a cause of this condition.

Q3628

A 68-year-old man reports a "missing spot" in his vision 1 week following cataract extraction by a first-year resident. Best corrected visual acuity is 20/100. In addition to normal postoperative findings, the examination is significant only for subtle foveal hypopigmentation. Macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrates the findings shown in the photo. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. photic retinopathy
Rationale
Nonexudative age-related macular degeneration, macular holes, and epiretinal membranes can all decrease central visual acuity; however, in the setting of recent (and likely prolonged) ophthalmic surgery with this supporting OCT, photic retinopathy secondary to exposure to the operating microscope light source is the most likely diagnosis. Although it is more common following retinal surgery, prolonged focal exposure can cause photochemical injury to the fovea, much like solar retinopathy. Patients typically present with central or paracentral scotomas, hypopigmented foveal lesions, and outer retinal cavitation. Most patients recover vision somewhat over a period of 3-6 months, typically to 20/25-20/40, but often with residual scotoma or metamorphopsia.

Q3629

A 32-year-old hyperope is referred for a second opinion regarding refractory central serous choroidopathy. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes subretinal fluid. There are no anterior chamber or vitreous cell abnormalities, and the patient reports no pain. A fluorescein angiogram reveals a "leopard spot" pattern of hyperfluorescence as shown. These findings indicate that the original diagnosis was incorrect. What is the correct diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. uveal effusion syndrome
Rationale
Uveal effusion syndrome is characterized by impaired posterior segment drainage, causing exudative detachment of the retina, choroid, or ciliary body. Young age, hyperopia, and nanophthalmos are risk factors. It can be mistakenly diagnosed as central serous choroidopathy. Examination findings include shifting subretinal fluid and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) hypertrophy. A fluorescein angiogram reveals a characteristic leopard spot appearance.
MEWDS does not typically present with exudative retinal or choroidal detachment. Although VKH can include exudative fluid and RPE changes, it typically includes a uveitic component, as well as constitutional signs, such as vitiligo and poliosis. Posterior scleritis would typically be painful.

Q3630

When treating the patient shown, which pharmaceutical agent is considered a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor analog or “VEGF trap”?
Correct answer: B. aflibercept
Rationale
The image demonstrates exudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Current therapies for exudative AMD are directed at inhibiting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), the cytokine most strongly implicated in the development of choroidal neovascularization. Aflibercept (Eylea) is nonspecific VEGF receptor analog referred to as VEGF trap. Ranibizumab (Lucentis) and bevacizumab (Avastin) bind to all isoforms of VEGF and are therefore nonspecific inhibitors of VEGF. Pegaptanib (Macugen) is an aptamer that binds to VEGF isoform 165.

Overall, 7%-18% of patients with acute, symptomatic PVD have retinal tears. However, 50%-70% of patients with acute PVD and vitreous hemorrhage have retinal tears. The risk of retinal tears in 7%-12% in patients with acute PVD without vitreous hemorrhage.

Q3632
Retina & Vitreous
What laboratory test should be performed in all black patients presenting with a traumatic hyphema?
Correct answer: B. sickle cell screening
Rationale
Sickle cell disease is an important risk factor for hyphema among persons of African descent. In the setting of high intraocular pressure (IOP) from hyphema and sickle cell disease, IOP-lowering medications, such as acetazolamide, would be relatively contraindicated, as they may precipitate a sickle cell crisis. A hypercoagulable state may lead to bleeding in the retina due to vascular occlusion, but it is not associated with hyphema.

Q3633
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common cause of decreased visual acuity in patients who present with acute central retinal vein occlusion?
Correct answer: B. macular edema
Rationale
Patients with acute central retinal vein occlusion commonly present with reduced visual acuity secondary to macular edema. Neovascularization of the iris usually occurs 3 to 5 months after the onset of symptoms. Peripheral ischemia with capillary dropout is seen in some severe cases of central retinal vein occlusion and can promote neovascularization, resulting in vitreous hemorrhage. Macular ischemia can occur as well but is a less likely cause of decreased acuity on presentation.

Q3634
Retina & Vitreous
An 80-year-old patient with painless vision loss has the finding pictured. What blood work is necessary in the initial evaluation?
Correct answer: D. erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Rationale
The image shows a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). No embolus can be seen.  Giant cell arteritis is the etiology of CRAO in 1%-2% of cases. Undetected and untreated, it represents a significant risk factor for second-eye involvement, with potentially devastating consequences. As such, an ESR should be obtained in all patients presenting with a CRAO.
Prothrombin time testing evaluates for the presence of a bleeding disorder, not a thrombotic disorder such as a CRAO. Hematocrit should be measured in cases of venous stasis. ANCA should be tested in cases of vasculitis.

Q3635
Retina & Vitreous
Which eyes are at greatest risk for the development of an RPE tear after anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy?
Correct answer: C. eyes with a fibrovascular pigment epithelial detachment (PED) > 600 µm in height
Rationale
Following anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy, both a pigment epithelial detachment greater than 600 μm in height and the presence of type 1 choroidal neovascularization (CNV), as evidenced by a fibrovascular component, increase the risk of an RPE tear. The mechanism might relate to contraction along the undersurface of the RPE monolayer as a result of the treatment.

Q3636
Retina & Vitreous
A 60-year-old reports gradual vision loss in the left eye and aching pain localized to the left orbit. Examination reveals iris neovascularization with an IOP of 11 mmHg, anterior chamber flare, scattered retinal blot hemorrhages, and dilated veins. The retinal artery collapses with gentle scleral depression. What is the most likely underlying etiology for this presentation?
Correct answer: D. carotid occlusive disease
Rationale
The patient’s presentation is consistent with ocular ischemic syndrome (OIS), which is most commonly due to carotid occlusive disease. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and radiation retinopathy can all cause retinal hemorrhages and iris neovascularization, but the retinal artery pressure is normal in all of those conditions. An eye with carotid occlusive disease will have low artery pressure, and the artery will therefore collapse easily with pressure on the globe. Despite a high rate of iris and angle neovascularization, 50% of patients with OIS have low or normal intraocular pressure, most likely caused by impaired aqueous production.

Q3637
Retina & Vitreous
In addition to choroidal rupture, what other conditions may result in posterior curvilinear rents in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/Bruch membrane complex?
Correct answer: B. angioid streaks
Rationale
Curvilinear breaks in the Bruch membrane are a component of traumatic choroidal rupture, high myopia (where they are known as "lacquer cracks"), and angioid streaks.
Ocular histoplasmosis syndrome rarely presents with a "histo streak," which is a curvilinear contiguous grouping of small chorioretinal scars or "histo spots." When present, these curvilinear scar groupings are in the near and far periphery, not in the posterior pole, where lacquer cracks and choroidal ruptures are more common, or near the optic disc, where angioid streaks are most common.
Age-related macular degeneration is associated with peripheral reticular pigment degeneration and choroidal neovascularization (which can breach the Bruch membrane) but does not lead to visible choroidal breaks.
Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy is an idiopathic inflammation of the choroid and retina. Bruch membrane or its rupture has not been implicated in its pathogenesis.

Q3638
Retina & Vitreous
What is the primary location of the intraocular hemorrhage of Valsalva retinopathy?
Correct answer: D. subinternal limiting membrane
Rationale
The primary location of the intraocular hemorrhage of Valsalva retinopathy is the subinternal limiting membrane space. The hemorrhage may also extend to the subretinal, subhyaloid, and/or vitreous spaces. Immediately following a Valsalva maneuver, a sudden rise in retinal venous pressure may cause the retinal capillaries to spontaneously rupture. The prognosis for Valsalva retinopathy is favorable with a course of observation. If spontaneous resolution does not occur, vitrectomy surgery may be considered.

Q3639
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most toxic intraocular metal?
Correct answer: D. copper
Rationale
Pure copper is acutely toxic to the retina, and prompt removal is required. Copper causes acute chalcosis, which manifests as severe inflammation and can lead to loss of the eye. If copper is alloyed with another metal so that the material has a final copper content of less than 85% (eg, brass, bronze), chronic chalcosis can occur. Iron is also toxic and can cause siderosis and vision loss, but this is subacute or chronic, unless an iron foreign body is infected. Zinc and aluminum tend to cause minimal inflammation and can become encapsulated, however, any very large foreign body can incite inflammation.

Q3640
Retina & Vitreous
What is a typical lesion size in multifocal choroiditis?
Correct answer: D. 50-200 microns
Rationale
In multifocal choroiditis, the choroidal lesions range from approximately 50 μm to 200 μm in diameter and are more typically located in the posterior fundus, concentrated in the macula and/or forming peripheral linear streaks. Active lesions appear as yellowish-white choroidal infiltrates and may be associated with a neurosensory retinal detachment, vascular sheathing, disc edema, and cystoid macular edema. Inactive lesions appear as variably pigmented, punched-out areas of chorioretinal atrophy.

Q3641
Retina & Vitreous
After examination of a 4-month-old baby with the findings shown, what is the next step?
Correct answer: A. immediate social service consultation
Rationale
Any physician who suspects that child abuse may have occurred is required by law in every US state and Canadian province to report the incident to a designated government agency.
Vitrectomy for vitreous hemorrhage may be required if amblyopia is likely to occur. Peripheral vitreous hemorrhage that does not occlude the central visual axis is unlikely to cause amblyopia.
ERG and FA may be done to determine the extent of damage, but these would not be done immediately.

Q3642
Retina & Vitreous
A 24-year-old man presents with decreased vision after blunt trauma. Examination reveals hemorrhagic chemosis, low intraocular pressure, and a hyphema. What is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: C. surgical exploration to identify and close the most posterior extent of the rupture
Rationale
The constellation of hemorrhagic chemosis, low intraocular pressure, and hyphema in the setting of blunt trauma should be considered scleral rupture until proven otherwise. Management includes primary exploration and closure of the anterior and posterior extents of the wound. Although 2 ruptures have been reported, this is rare. If the rupture extends near the extraocular muscles, disinsertion with placement of interrupted sutures may be necessary.
Often the vision is extremely poor (hand motions or light perception), but primary enucleation would be considered if the vision were reliably no light perception. Electroretinography has no place in the management of this patient. Similarly, expectant observation would only be considered if the patient were prohibited from surgical intervention because of traumatic neurosurgical or other emergent instability.

Q3643
Retina & Vitreous
A 70-year-old man with poor visual acuity since childhood comes for a routine exam. His visual acuity is 20/200. The maculas appear mildly atrophic but lack any fluid on optical coherence tomography (OCT). There are irregular clumps of pigment in the peripheral retinas. The ophthalmologist obtains old records describing an electronegative electroretinogram (ERG). His daughter’s 10-year-old son recently had “bleeding from some kind of retina problem.” What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. juvenile X-linked retinoschisis
Rationale
Juvenile X-linked retinoschisis (XLRS) is a rare hereditary condition in which visual acuity typically decreases to the 20/200 level. A classic finding in XLRS is a “spoke wheel” pattern of radial striae in the central macula, with accompanying schisis. Macular schisis is not a universal finding, however, and the schisis cavities may close with age. The absence of macular schisis thus does not rule out this diagnosis. An electronegative ERG, in which the b-wave is reduced, is also a feature of XLRS. Peripheral retinoschisis is present in up to 50% of patients, and peripheral pigmentation is also a common feature. X-linked inheritance is implied by the family history, because the patient’s daughter would be an obligate carrier and her sons would have a 50% chance of being affected. Mild trauma in boys with XLRS can cause vitreous hemorrhage related to shearing of vessels in areas of peripheral retinoschisis. The history and clinical features in this patient are thus suggestive of XLRS.
Genetic testing can provide a definitive diagnosis. The electronegative ERG distinguishes XLRS from other hereditary conditions that may have some isolated overlapping examination features. Macular schisis is also a common feature of enhanced S-cone syndrome, but this autosomal recessive disorder lacks an electronegative ERG. In addition, pigmentary deposits are classically located around the arcades rather than more peripherally and patients can maintain good central visual acuity. Retinitis pigmentosa, which can be X-linked, is not accompanied by an electronegative ERG. Finally, although advanced Best disease may be characterized by poor visual acuity and macular atrophy, peripheral pigmentation is absent and the ERG is normal.

Q3644
Retina & Vitreous
When is observation without treatment of a retinal flap tear appropriate?
Correct answer: D. when a pigmented demarcation line is present
Rationale
A demarcation line is a pigmentary reaction that can slowly develop around a retinal break that has not progressed to a retinal detachment. The presence of a demarcation line suggests chronicity of the break and a low likelihood of progression to a retinal detachment, particularly in the absence of symptoms. Such a break can be observed. The presence of hemorrhage is characteristic of an acute retinal break, and represents an indication to treat. The presence of subretinal fluid suggests a tendency for the break to progress to a retinal detachment, and is again an indication to treat.

Q3645
Retina & Vitreous
The Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) demonstrated a benefit of specific nutritional supplements for what category of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?
Correct answer: D. bilateral intermediate or unilateral advanced nonexudative AMD
Rationale
The AREDS demonstrated a benefit of antioxidant (beta-carotene and vitamin E) and zinc nutritional supplementation for bilateral intermediate or unilateral advanced nonexudative AMD. The AREDS did not detect effectiveness for bilateral advanced nonexudative AMD, bilateral early nonexudative AMD, or exudative AMD. Because the study endpoint was the development of choroidal neovascularization, the study was not designed to assess or include any bilateral exudative AMD subjects.

Q3646
Retina & Vitreous
What is the term for an elongated, redundant segment of retinal tissue that extends onto the pars plana?
Correct answer: D. meridional fold
Rationale
Meridional folds are folds of redundant retina, usually located superonasally. They are usually associated with dentate processes but may also extend posteriorly from ora bays. Normal thickness retinal extensions that interrupt the contour of the ora serrata are referred to as dentate processes or retinal "teeth." Between the dentate processes are the ora bays of pars plana epithelium. Peripheral tufts and zonular traction tufts are found more posteriorly in the retina.

Q3647
Retina & Vitreous
Nine weeks after routine cataract surgery, a patient develops a steroid-responsive granulomatous uveitis/endophthalmitis, with a white plaque on her intraocular lens. What would be the most appropriate management of this condition?
Correct answer: B. pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and partial capsulectomy with intravitreal antibiotic injection
Rationale
The clinical history is characteristic of Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis. Although injection of intravitreous antibiotics may clear the infection in up to 50% of cases, an appropriate management is pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) with partial capsulectomy and antibiotic injection. Occasionally, removal of the intraocular lens and the entire capsular bag is required to definitively treat the condition. Sampling the anterior chamber, especially the vitreous, is the usual approach for identification of the causative microbe, not for management of the condition. However, because P acnes is an obligate microaerophilic bacterium, it may not survive in a culture unless that culture is maintained in a low-oxygen environment. Thus, the culture positivity rate is low. Topical antibiotics and steroids will treat the symptoms, but will not eradicate the infection.

Q3648
Retina & Vitreous
A patient develops a spontaneous vitreous hemorrhage. In what setting would immediate surgical intervention be indicated?
Correct answer: D. 63-year-old patient with prior cataract surgery and a retinal detachment demonstrated on B-scan ultrasonography
Rationale
The most likely etiology of a vitreous hemorrhage in a 63-year-old pseudophake is a posterior vitreous separation with a possible retinal tear or detachment. If visualization of the retinal periphery is precluded by the vitreous hemorrhage, and if B-scan ultrasonography demonstrates a retinal detachment in such a patient, prompt surgical intervention is indicated for repair of the retinal detachment. Vitreous hemorrhage associated with PDR, BRVO, or an eccentric disciform process in the absence of a retinal detachment does not represent an urgent situation and may be cautiously monitored for spontaneous clearing prior to performing definitive therapy. If vitreous hemorrhage does not clear within a reasonable time frame, intervention with vitrectomy surgery may be considered.

Q3649
Retina & Vitreous
What is a characteristic feature of choroidal rupture?
Correct answer: B. typically occurs concentric to the optic disc
Rationale
When the eye is compressed along its anterior-posterior axis, tears might occur in the Bruch membrane, which has little elasticity, as well as in the overlying RPE and fibrous tissue investing the choriocapillaris. Adjacent subretinal hemorrhage is common. Choroidal ruptures occur typically in the periphery and concentric to the optic disc. There is no effective treatment for choroidal rupture.

Q3650
Retina & Vitreous
In patients with intermediate or advanced age-related macular degeneration (AMD), to what degree did the nutritional supplementation used in the AREDS (Age-Related Eye Disease Study) reduce the risk for progression to more-advanced stages of AMD?
Correct answer: C. 25%
Rationale
In the AREDS (Age-Related Eye Disease Study), nutritional supplementation with the antioxidant vitamins C (500 mg) and E (400 IU), beta carotene (15 mg), and the micronutrient zinc (80 mg zinc oxide and 2 mg cupric oxide to prevent zinc-induced anemia) in patients with intermediate or advanced AMD showed a 25% risk reduction for progression to more-advanced stages of AMD and a 19% risk reduction in rates of moderate vision loss (3 lines of visual acuity) at 5 years. In the AREDS 2 Study, replacing beta carotene with lutein and zeaxanthin yielded very similar results.

Q3651
Retina & Vitreous
What hemoglobinopathy mutation carries the highest risk for severe retinopathy?
Correct answer: B. hemoglobin S-thalassemia
Rationale
Sickle-cell hemoglobinopathies are common in the US black population, but the prevalence rate of proliferative sickle retinopathy varies greatly by mutation. For instance, 8% of African Americans carry the sickle gene (genotype hemoglobin AS). Proliferative disease is rare in this large group. In contrast, neovascularization of the retina has been reported in as high as 33% of SC patients and up to 14% of S-thalassemia patients. Although rare, thalassemia frequently causes retinopathy. Proliferative disease is found rarely in AC and in only 3% of SS affected patients.

Q3652
Retina & Vitreous
What intervention is indicated in the initial management of a patient with a penetrating ocular injury and possible intraocular foreign body?
Correct answer: A. computed tomography (CT) scan
Rationale
In a patient with a penetrating ocular injury and possible intraocular foreign body (IOFB), prompt detection of an IOFB may change therapy. A CT scan would be extremely useful in this setting to identify if a radiodense IOFB is present. Direct pressure on the injured globe from scleral depression is contraindicated. When an IOFB is a possibility, MRI is contraindicated, as the effect of a magnetic field on a ferrous IOFB could result in additional intraocular trauma. There is no proven benefit to the immediate administration of intravitreal corticosteroids in the setting of acute penetrating ocular injuries.

Q3653
Retina & Vitreous
In a patient diagnosed with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSR), what finding might initiate reconsideration of the diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. intraretinal fluid
Rationale
CSR is characterized by the presence of retinal pigment epithelial detachments, serous retinal detachments, and macular or inferior peripheral pigmentary changes. Optical coherence tomography might be used to demonstrate the pigment epithelial detachment and subretinal fluid. However, CSR is not associated with intraretinal fluid. If intraretinal fluid is discovered, either the diagnosis of CSR is incorrect or the patient has developed the complication of CSR-associated choroidal neovascularization.

Q3654
Retina & Vitreous
During a routine eye examination for an asymptomatic patient, the finding shown in the image is identified. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this pathology?
Correct answer: D. observation
Rationale
Observation is the appropriate treatment for an asymptomatic atrophic retinal hole in the absence of an associated retinal detachment. Scleral buckle, laser, and/or cryopexy are not typically indicated in this setting.

Q3655
Retina & Vitreous
A 26-year-old, previously healthy pregnant woman reports visual changes. Her medical and surgical history is unremarkable. She says she sees flashes on and off, and at times floaters. She denies any trauma or injury. She places her head on the chin rest of the slit lamp, and the ophthalmologist notices that she has facial swelling. The fundoscopic examination is shown. What is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: A. Refer the patient directly to the emergency department.
Rationale
An acute hypertensive episode may produce focal intraretinal periarteriolar transudates, which are shown in this image. Severe preeclampsia requires emergent intervention to reduce morbidity and avoid mortality, so the most appropriate management would be to send the patient to the emergency department immediately.
A CT scan would not be useful in this case and would waste precious time. Based on the patient's age and the fundoscopic examination, it is unlikely that she has a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), and would therefore not require an examination with scleral depression. The management of her hypertension and edema could require a diuretic but would not change the acute course of her disease, which necessitates inpatient management with an obstetrician trained for high-risk pregnancies.

Q3656
Retina & Vitreous
What is the mode of inheritance for Von Hippel–Lindau syndrome?
Correct answer: B. autosomal dominant
Rationale
Von Hippel–Lindau syndrome is caused by a tumor suppressor gene mutation on the short arm of chromosome 3 (3p26–p25), the inheritance of which is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance and variable expression.

Q3657
Retina & Vitreous
Compared with conventional macular photocoagulation, what is an advantage of subthreshold (barely visible to invisible) laser treatment?
Correct answer: B. has the potential to reduce the number and size of scotomas
Rationale
Compared with conventional macular photocoagulation, delivery systems that apply subthreshold (barely visible to invisible) laser spots have the potential to reduce the number and size of scotomas, although this benefit has not been definitively demonstrated in randomized controlled trials. The shorter laser-energy pulses result in less or no thermal damage. However, titrating the amount of treatment is rendered difficult by the lack of visible feedback.

Q3658
Retina & Vitreous
A patient who experiences an acute subarachnoid hemorrhage is found to have loss of vision and vitreous hemorrhage. What pathophysiologic process is implicated?
Correct answer: B. acute rise in intraocular venous pressure
Rationale
The clinical presentation is consistent with Terson syndrome, which is caused by abrupt intracranial hemorrhage. The mechanism is suspected to be that the hemorrhage causes an acute rise in the intraocular venous pressure, resulting in a rupture of peripapillary and retinal vessels. Granulocyte aggregation, leukoembolization, and fat embolization are not thought to be causative or contributory factors in Terson syndrome. They are, however, thought to play roles in the pathogenesis of Purtscher and Purtscher-like retinopathy.

Q3659
Retina & Vitreous
What is the innermost anatomic layer of the neurosensory retina?
Correct answer: B. internal limiting membrane
Rationale
The internal limiting membrane (ILM) is the innermost anatomic layer of the neurosensory retina. This acellular membrane is the boundary between the retina and the vitreous body, formed by astrocytes and the end feet of Müller cells. The photoreceptor, inner nuclear, and ganglion cell layers are all located external to the ILM.

Q3660
Retina & Vitreous
What complication is seen more often after laser photocoagulation for proliferative sickle cell retinopathy than for diabetic proliferative retinopathy?
Correct answer: D. retinal detachment
Rationale
Retinal tears and subsequent rhegmatogenous retinal detachment can occur after peripheral laser photocoagulation to treat proliferative sickle cell retinopathy. Retinal tears occur more commonly after laser treatment in proliferative sickle cell retinopathy than in diabetic proliferative retinopathy. Reduced peripheral vision, choroidal detachments, and vitreous hemorrhage may occur after laser photocoagulation but do not have a specific predilection for sickle cell retinopathy.

Q3661
Retina & Vitreous
A patient has a history of idiopathic macular hole in the right eye. The left eye has a posterior vitreous detachment. What is the risk of getting an idiopathic macular hole in the left eye?
Correct answer: A. The left eye is not at any increased risk of developing a macular hole.
Rationale
Idiopathic macular holes develop in both eyes in 10% of patients.
A complete posterior vitreous detachment lowers the risk of developing an idiopathic macular hole.
Fellow eyes of patients with idiopathic macular holes are at an increased risk compared to the general population, unless there is a complete posterior vitreous detachment.
Idiopathic macular holes are most prevalent in older age groups.

Q3662
Retina & Vitreous
What clinical finding best characterizes Coats disease?
Correct answer: B. vascular dilatation
Rationale
Coats disease is characterized by the presence of vascular dilatations (retinal telangiectasia), including ectatic arterioles, microaneurysms, venous dilations (phlebectasias), and fusiform capillary dilatations, which are frequently associated with exudative retinal detachment. Usually only 1 eye is involved, and there is a marked male predominance (85%). To date, researchers have not identified an associated gene or chromosome or any hereditary pattern, and no association between Coats disease and systemic disease has been found. In an eye with Coats disease, the abnormal vessels are compromised, resulting in the leakage of serum and other blood components, which accumulate in and under the retina. Any portion of the peripheral and macular capillary system may be involved. Although angiography demonstrates the presence of retinal capillary nonperfusion, posterior segment neovascularization is unusual.

Q3663
Retina & Vitreous
What is the maximum daily dose of hydroxychloroquine that has been recommended to minimize the risk of retinopathy?
Correct answer: C. 5.0 mg/kg/day using total body mass
Rationale
The most recent data suggests that a dose of 5.0 mg/kg of real body weight may be the safest recommendation. Previous reviews had suggested the use of a calculation involving lean body weight, based on concerns that the drug does not penetrate lipid rich tissues. Per the AAO 2016 statement “High dose and long duration of use are the most significant risks. Other major factors are concomitant renal disease, or use of tamoxifen.” And “At recommended doses, the risk of toxicity up to 5 years is under 1% and up to 10 years is under 2%, but it rises to almost 20% after 20 years. However, even after 20 years, a patient without toxicity has only a 4% risk of converting in the subsequent year.”

Q3664
Retina & Vitreous
What systemic disease causes the fundus appearance shown in the image?
Correct answer: B. hypertension
Rationale
Systemic hypertension may cause retinopathy, choroidopathy, and optic neuropathy. The most severe manifestation is optic neuropathy, which presents as optic disc edema, hemorrhages, and ischemia. Optic disc manifestations suggest a sustained and highly elevated systolic blood pressure, often above 200 mm Hg.
Ocular ischemic syndrome comprises the ocular symptoms and signs attributable to chronic severe ocular hypoperfusion caused by ipsilateral carotid obstruction or ophthalmic artery obstruction. Typical findings include narrowed arteries, dilated by not very tortuous veins, hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and neovascularization of the optic nerve head, retina, or both.
Diabetic retinopathy is characterized by intraretinal hemorrhages, microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, and dilation and beading of retinal veins. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is defined by extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation.
Aortic dissection is associated with Marfan syndrome and does not have a characteristic fundus appearance.

Q3665
Retina & Vitreous
What autosomal dominant condition produces fundus changes similar to those of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?
Correct answer: C. familial exudative vitreoretinopathy
Rationale
Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) is usually inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, but X-linked transmission also occurs. It is characterized by failure of the temporal retina to vascularize and is phenotypically similar to ROP. Unlike patients with ROP, individuals with FEVR are born full term and have normal respiratory status. In FEVR, the peripheral retinal vessels are dragged, straightened, and end abruptly a variable distance from the ora.
Norrie disease and incontinentia pigmenti are transmitted as X-linked traits. Persistent fetal vasculature is not inherited.

Q3666
Retina & Vitreous
Given that diabetic retinopathy may worsen in severity after cataract surgery, what treatment should be considered for patients with severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) prior to cataract extraction, if the media is sufficiently clear?
Correct answer: A. panretinal photocoagulation
Rationale
The risk of progression in patients with severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy or proliferative diabetic retinopathy can be reduced by performing pre-cataract panretinal photocoagulation if the view of the posterior segment is sufficiently clear. In addition, diabetic macular edema (DME), sometimes undetected prior to cataract removal, can manifest or worsen following cataract surgery in patients with diabetes mellitus. Ideally, cataract surgery should be delayed until macular edema has resolved.
Clinicians may also consider preoperative focal laser, intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF), or  intravitreal steroid injection for patients with center-involved DME. Topical NSAIDs (not corticosteroids) used perioperatively may also decrease the incidence of postoperative DME in diabetic patients. Focal laser photocoagulation has no effect on the progression of proliferative diabetic retinopathy following cataract surgery. A pupillary iridotomy is not indicated in cases of cataracts with diabetic retinopathy.
Whether an IOL, of any material, is implanted has little effect on diabetic retinopathy. Similarly, the likelihood of progression of proliferative retinopathy is not affected by the technique chosen for phacoemulsification.

Q3667
Retina & Vitreous
In humans, what ocular disease is most conclusively linked to autoantibodies directed against retinal antigens?
Correct answer: B. cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR)
Rationale
CAR has been closely linked to several autoantibodies, including antienolase and antirecoverin. The other 3 inflammatory conditions listed (VKH, MEWDS, HLA-B27–associated acute anterior uveitis) are not known to be associated with any specific antibody, although they are presumed to be autoimmune in origin. Rationale
An epiretinal membrane is a fibrocellular membrane that adheres on the internal limiting membrane of the posterior pole, usually surrounding or just eccentric to the fovea. Contracture of this membrane can cause tangential forces on the inner retina, which may manifest as a sheen with wrinkling or striae, as well as increased vascular tortuosity or straightening of the retinal vessels. Resultant distortion of retinal surface architecture can cause metamorphopsia and reduced visual acuity.

The Diabetic Retinopathy Study demonstrated that panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) was effective in treating retinal and high-risk neovascularization on the disc or retina from proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). Rationale
For lacerating wounds that extend far posteriorly and make visualization and suturing difficult, the safest course of action is to leave the most posterior aspect to heal without sutures. Continuing to dissect and attempt to suture risks causing extrusion of ocular contents and further damage. Most surgeons do not think that immediate vitrectomy is indicated in an open-globe injury. Removing vitreous to soften the eye to facilitate suturing should be not done. Fibrin sealant should not be used to close an open globe injury.

Q3676

What bilateral white dot syndrome is characterized by profound vision loss typically followed by full or near-full vision recovery?
Correct answer: A. acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)
Rationale
Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) is an uncommon, usually bilateral inflammatory disorder characterized by acute onset visual loss, usually followed weeks to months later by substantial or near-complete improvement. On FA, APMPPE (also known as AMPPE or AMPPPE) in the acute phase demonstrates a characteristic fundus pattern of early lesion blockage, followed by lesion staining in the middle and late phases. No treatment has been demonstrated to affect the time or final outcome of recovery. Birdshot uveitis is characterized by insidious onset and chronic progression. Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is a unilateral syndrome with decreased vision, scotomas, and sometimes photopsias, with improvement over 2-6 weeks without treatment. Serpiginous chorioretinopathy is typically relentlessly progressive, and destroys the RPE on photoreceptors. Thus, recovery of vision, even following immunosuppression, is atypical.

What is the predominant mode of inheritance of Stargardt disease/fundus flavimaculatus?

Rationale
Stargardt disease is the most common juvenile macular dystrophy and a common cause of central vision loss in adults younger than 50 years. The visual acuity in Stargardt disease typically ranges from 20/50 to 20/200. The classic Stargardt phenotype is characterized by a juvenile-onset foveal atrophy surrounded by discrete, yellowish, round or pisciform flecks at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The vast majority of Stargardt disease is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. This includes those cases caused by mutations in an adenosine 5'-triphosphate (ATP)-binding cassette transporter protein (ABCA4). Rarer forms of Stargardt disease may be inherited as an autosomal dominant pattern (PRPH2).

Rationale
Sickle cell retinopathy can cause visual symptoms for a number of reasons, including vitreous hemorrhage, macular ischemia, vascular occlusions, and retinal detachment. Visual symptoms are most frequently caused by vitreous hemorrhage derived from the retinal neovascularization. Occlusive vascular changes and an enlarged foveal avascular zone (FAZ) are common in patients with sickle cell retinopathy but may not produce symptoms. Retinal detachments, whether rhegmatogenous, tractional, or combined, can occur but are not the most common cause of visual symptoms.

For a patient with lattice degeneration, what is the strongest additional indication for treating with laser retinopexy and/or cryopexy?
Correct answer: A. symptomatic retinal tear with or without a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD)
Rationale
A symptomatic retinal tear would convey the highest risk of retinal detachment and would therefore be the strongest indication for laser retinopexy and/or cryopexy in a patient with lattice degeneration whether with or without a precipitating PVD. Asymptomatic atrophic retinal holes without surrounding subretinal fluid, asymptomatic atrophic retinal holes with limited surrounding subretinal fluid and a prominent demarcation line, and multiple rows of lattice degeneration without retinal breaks represent lower-risk situations for progression to clinical retinal detachment. Treatment is rarely indicated in these circumstances. A history of retinal detachment in the other eye that was caused by a lattice related tear or atrophic hole may increase the appropriateness to treat lattice lesions with atrophic holes with or without fluid.

Rationale
The clinical presentation is consistent with moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) without macular edema. Optimization of glycemic control has been shown to slow the progression of disease at this stage. The 2019 AAO Preferred Practice Pattern does not advise fluorescein angiography (FA) as part of the regular examination of diabetic patients. In patients with severe NPDR or proliferative diabetic retinopathy, however, FA can be a valuable tool in indicating the severity of retinal ischemia and identifying clinically occult neovascularization. Neither prophylactic scatter laser photocoagulation nor low-dose aspirin has been proven to benefit this disease stage.

Correct answer: B. pars plana vitrectomy with removal of the foreign body
Rationale
This patient's clinical history is consistent with a penetrating ocular injury by a retained intraocular foreign body. Management consists of pars plana vitrectomy, foreign body removal, repair of associated injuries (scleral laceration, traumatic cataract, retinal tear, etc.), and administration of intravitreal antibiotics. This treatment regimen is most safely and effectively performed in the controlled setting of the operating room.

Q3685

A 29-year-old man presents for routine ophthalmic examination. He notes poor vision in his left eye for "as long as he can remember," but he has never had an eye examination in the past. Visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye is unremarkable. Fundus examination of the left eye is depicted in the figure. What would a fluorescein angiogram, if performed, be most likely to demonstrate?
Correct answer: B. no leakage, as well as a gravitational plasma-erythrocyte separation
Rationale
The figure depicts a retinal cavernous hemangioma, which is a benign hamartoma. Most cases are sporadic, although a familial, autosomal dominant pattern has been seen in conjunction with skin and intracranial hemangiomas. Clinically, a retinal cavernous hemangioma appears as a grape-like cluster of thin-walled saccular angiomatous lesions in the inner retina or optic nerve. They are typically located peripherally and are asymptomatic (this patient has a severe case involving the central vision that is less common). Rarely, the hemangiomas may bleed into the vitreous. This lesion should be on the differential diagnosis of any patient with a vitreous hemorrhage of unknown etiology. In addition, cavernous hemangiomas are one of the conditions that can cause subretinal, intraretinal, and preretinal hemorrhage. Blood flow through the lesions is slow.
Fluorescein angiography typically shows no leakage and may show gravitational plasma-erythrocyte separation. Subretinal edema and exudate is uncommon. Most lesions are observed unless they cause vision loss, in which case cryotherapy or photocoagulation may be considered. If severe vitreous hemorrhage occurs, pars plana vitrectomy is an option.

Rationale
Vascular, malignant, and inflammatory disorders are the most common causes of exudative retinal detachment, which is the diagnosis in this case. What finding most supports a working diagnosis of ocular toxoplasmosis infection?

Rationale
Acute focal chorioretinitis adjacent to an old chorioretinal scar supports a working diagnosis of ocular toxoplasmosis infection. Positive serum IgG antibody titer is only indicative of previous exposure to T gondii (recent or past), and is not specific for active disease. T gondii is a protozoan, not a bacterium, and is not typically isolable from a vitreous specimen.

Q3694

A patient develops branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) at a site other than an arteriovenous crossing. What underlying etiology should be considered?
Correct answer: C. vasculitis
Rationale
In branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO), obstruction of the vein occurs most commonly at an arteriovenous crossing, where thickening of the arterial wall compresses the adjacent vein within a common adventitial sheath. When the occlusion does not occur at an arteriovenous crossing, the possibility of an underlying retinochoroiditis or retinal vasculitis should be considered. Hypertension and glaucoma are risk factors for BRVO but are not implicated in occlusion at sites other than arteriovenous crossings. An embolus may cause a retinal artery occlusion but not a retinal vein occlusion.

Q3695
Retina & Vitreous
Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is most commonly seen in what disease (from most to least common)?
Correct answer: D. SC > SThal > SS
Rationale
Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is most commonly seen with SC > SThal > SS disease. Sickle cell results from a defective allele of hemoglobin A. In SC disease, the valine is substituted for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta-polypeptide chain. Peripheral arteriolar occlusion and capillary nonperfusion of the retina may occur, which may lead to peripheral "sea-fan" retinal neovascularization at the border of perfused and nonperfused retina. Treatment is laser photocoagulation to areas of ischemic retina. However, treatment is not recommended directly to "sea fans," as retinal tears and hemorrhage may result.
Complications of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy include vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment. Nonproliferative sickle cell retinopathy may present as salmon-patch hemorrhages (intraretinal hemorrhage after arteriolar occlusion), refractile/iridescent deposits (resorbed hemorrhage with hemosiderin deposits within the inner retina), or black sunburst lesions (retinal pigment epithelium [RPE] hypertrophy/hyperplasia from prior hemorrhage). In addition, patients can develop spontaneous vascular occlusions of large retinal arteries. Another eye finding is the "comma sign." Many comma-shaped thrombi dilate and occlude the conjunctival capillaries. They are most commonly seen in the inferior bulbar conjunctiva. Similarly, segmentation of blood vessels may be seen on the optic disc as the "disc sign."

Pneumatic retinopexy is contraindicated in the presence of PVR. Laser demarcation is not effective for a total retinal detachment. Scleral buckle alone is typically not effective in the presence of multiple posterior retinal breaks.

Q3707
Retina & Vitreous
For a patient with age-related macular degeneration and initial, new-onset metamorphopsia, what is the most reasonable sequence of ancillary testing?
Correct answer: B. spectral domain optical coherence tomography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, fluorescein angiography
Rationale
Although controversy exists as to whether intravenous fundus fluorescein angiography (FA) or optical coherence tomography (OCT) is more sensitive in detecting exudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FA may be necessary in this setting, as it may diagnose the retinal macroaneurysm, pseudophakic macular edema, branch retinal vein occlusion, and other confounders. However, there is no controversy about our goal to initially use the safest and least invasive diagnostic modality. Thus, the most reasonable sequence would be to do OCT before angiography in this setting. In straightforward cases, spectral domain OCT may be the only ancillary testing needed to initially diagnose a new case of exudative AMD. Once neovascularization is confirmed and/or other confounders excluded, OCT is very useful to noninvasively monitor response to therapy.
Fundus photography is excellent at documenting the macula examination on a particular day but does not provide additional diagnostic information like the other modalities listed. Autofluorescence is very useful in assessing the health of the RPE and the accumulation of lipofuscin but is not helpful in assessing initial metamorphopsia as OCT or even FA.

Q3708
Retina & Vitreous
Laser photocoagulation is indicated for what complication of acquired retinal macroaneurysm?
Correct answer: B. macular edema
Rationale
Focal laser photocoagulation is indicated for visually significant macular edema associated with acquired retinal arteriolar macroaneurysm. Dense vitreous hemorrhage and, less commonly, extensive subretinal hemorrhage, may be managed with vitrectomy surgery when clinically indicated. Retinal neovascularization is not a common complication of acquired retinal arteriolar macroaneurysm.

Q3709
Retina & Vitreous
A patient presenting with a posterior vitreous detachment with pigment granules in the anterior vitreous (Shafer sign) is approximately how much more likely to have a retinal break than a patient without this presentation?
Correct answer: A. 7 times
Rationale
Patients presenting with an acute posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) and pigment granules in the anterior vitreous, also known as a positive "Shafer sign" or "tobacco dust," are roughly 7 times more likely to have an associated retinal break than patients with PVD without pigment granules.

Q3710
Retina & Vitreous
Intravitreal bevacizumab has demonstrated efficacy in the management of diabetic macular edema and what other ophthalmic disorder?
Correct answer: D. choroidal neovascularization
Rationale
Anti–vascular epithelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) drugs, including bevacizumab, have been shown to be efficacious in treatment of choroidal neovascular membrane. Bevacizumab has no role in treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis, central serous chorioretinopathy, or choroidal effusion.

Q3711
Retina & Vitreous
What traumatic extraocular condition is associated with a branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO)?
Correct answer: C. femur fracture
Rationale
A BRAO is the result of embolization or thrombosis of the affected vessel. Common sources of emboli include cholesterol emboli arising in the carotid arteries, platelet-fibrin emboli associated with large vessel arteriosclerosis, and calcific emboli arising from diseased cardiac valves.
Rare causes of a BRAO include emboli resulting from cardiac myxoma, fat emboli from long-bone fractures, septic emboli from infective endocarditis, and talc emboli from intravenous (IV) drug use.
Traumatic pancreatitis is associated with Purtscher retinopathy, which is associated with focal areas of retina whitening that may superficially resemble a BRAO, but is not a BRAO. Subarachnoid hemorrhage may be associated with intraocular hemorrhage or Terson syndrome.

Q3712
Retina & Vitreous
What two adhesion molecules attach the vitreous to the internal limiting membrane (ILM) of the retinal surface?
Correct answer: D. fibronectin and laminin
Rationale
The vitreous attaches to the internal limiting membrane (ILM) of the retinal surface primarily via fibronectin and laminin. The integrin molecule has been shown to induce posterior vitreous detachment, not facilitate attachment. The connectin molecule does not appear to play a significant role in vitreoretinal adhesion.

Q3713
Retina & Vitreous
What organism causes cat-scratch disease?
Correct answer: D. Bartonella henselae
Rationale
Bartonella henselae

Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae.
Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, which can result in irritation and inflammation of the eye and swelling of lymph glands near the ear. Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease.

Q3714
Retina & Vitreous
During evaluation of a patient with bilateral blurry vision of several weeks' duration, the ophthalmologist identifies bilateral macular edema with microaneurysms, neovascularization of the optic discs, and diffuse peripheral cotton wool spots and intraretinal hemorrhages. The patient reports a previous history of nasopharyngeal cancer. Blood glucose and HbA1C levels are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
Correct answer: D. radiation retinopathy
Rationale
In the setting of nasopharyngeal cancer, the diagnosis of radiation retinopathy is the most likely. Radiation retinopathy shares features of deep and superficial retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and microaneurysms, and retinal and/or optic nerve neovascularization, much like other microangiopathic retinal vascular disorders such as diabetic and sickle cell retinopathies. Typically, an exposure of at least 30-35 grays (Gy) of radiation is needed to develop signs of radiation retinopathy, although it may develop after as little as 15 Gy of external beam radiation. Findings usually manifest approximately 18 months following external beam radiation, although they may be present earlier, following plaque brachytherapy.

Q3715
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common isolate from patients with filtering bleb-associated endophthalmitis?
Correct answer: C. Streptococcus species
Rationale
Streptococcus species

Streptococcus species are the most common organisms isolated in bleb-associated endophthalmitis. This endophthalmitis may occur months to years following the primary operative procedure. Treatment is the same as for other forms of bacterial endophthalmitis. Given the greater virulence of Streptococcus species, the prognosis is more guarded. Staphylococcus species are less commonly the cause of this form of endophthalmitis. Candida albicans rarely is a causative organism, and herpes simplex is not a cause of bleb-associated endophthalmitis.

Q3716
Retina & Vitreous
A 62-year-old woman presents with decreased central vision. An optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan is performed and the image is shown below. What complication is most likely to occur?
Correct answer: D. macular hole
Rationale
The clinical presentation described is consistent with the vitreomacular traction syndrome (VMT), also known as vitreomacular adhesion (VMA). VMT is a disorder of the vitreoretinal interface, characterized by (a) an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), (b) an abnormally strong adherence of the posterior hyaloid face to the macula, and (c) anteroposterior traction exerted by the vitreous pulling at adherent sites on the macula, causing morphologic and possible visual symptoms. Focal attachment of the vitreous to the foveola can induce foveal cavitation and macular hole formation.
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments can be caused by retinal breaks or tears that form during a posterior vitreous detachment. The scan shows VMT and an incomplete PVD, so this would be less likely.
VMT is not directly related to the development of choroidal neovascularization or peripheral retinoschisis.

Q3717
Retina & Vitreous
For a patient with initial onset of symptoms due to central serous choroidopathy, what is the preferred management?
Correct answer: D. observation with close monitoring
Rationale
Central serous chorioretinopathy typically resolves spontaneously within weeks to months of onset. Persistent, symptomatic cases may respond to thermal laser photocoagulation and/or verteporfin photodynamic therapy. Systemic corticosteroid therapy may exacerbate the condition, as may systemic conditions associated with elevated serum cortisol levels.
