What vitreoretinal surgical technique is contraindicated in the management of tractional detachment in a patient with the retinal findings shown?
Correct answer: C. scleral buckling
Rationale
The photo shown demonstrates "sea fan" neovascularization, a hallmark of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy. Placement of encircling scleral buckles has been associated with risk of anterior segment ischemia and/or necrosis in this patient population.

Q3719
Retina & Vitreous
A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is under treatment with hydroxychloroquine. What factor places her at greatest risk of visual loss from toxicity?
Correct answer: C. renal insufficiency
Rationale
Because hydroxychloroquine is metabolized in the kidneys and liver, patients with renal insufficiency, such as those with lupus nephritis and diabetic nephropathy, are at increased risk for accumulation of toxic metabolites. Older patients are at greater risk than younger patients. The most recent data suggest that a hydroxychloroquine dosage of 5.0 mg/kg/day and a chloroquine dosage of 2.3 mg/kg/day based on the patient’s real body weight may be safer across all body mass indexes than the dosage recommendation of 6.5 mg/kg/day and 3 mg/kg/day, respectively using the patient’s ideal body weight. Glaucoma is not a risk factor. Other risk factors, not given as choices here, include higher dose and total dose of hydroxychloroquine.

Q3720
Retina & Vitreous
What peripheral retinal lesion is least likely to be associated with retinal tear or detachment?
Correct answer: B. paving-stone degeneration
Rationale
Paving-stone degeneration is not associated with increased retinal detachment risk because it does not affect the vitreoretinal interface, and histologically represents fusion or fibrosis of the retina with the choroid similar to laser or cryopexy treatment. It is important to distinguish between paving-stone degeneration and a localized spot of atrophy from a hole or tear associated with a cuff of subretinal fluid and subjacent retinal pigment epithelial atrophy.  Lattice degeneration is among the peripheral retinal lesions most associated with increased risk of retinal detachment. Meridional folds can develop a tear at the posterior edge of the fold, and zonular traction tufts are a cause of small retinal flap tears, often seen following cataract surgery.

Q3721
Retina & Vitreous
A 6-year-old boy presents for evaluation of decreased vision in his right eye, and is found to have a vitreous hemorrhage. His mother notes that there is a history of an eye condition on her side of the family. Fundus examination of the fellow eye, as well as the eyes of the patient's asymptomatic brother, identifies fine radial striae involving the maculae. What gene encodes the defective protein responsible for the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
Correct answer: C. RS1
Rationale
RS1

In concert, vitreous hemorrhage, a male relative with fine radial folds in the maculae, and a maternal family history of eye disease are all suggestive of x-linked retinoschisis (XLRS). The gene involved in this condition is RS1, which encodes the adhesion protein retinoschisin, which is responsible for Müller cell integrity. Boys with congenital XLRS frequently present with vitreous hemorrhages from torn retinal vessels in areas of retinoschisis. Foveal schisis presents with small cystic spaces and fine radial striae in the central maculae, although patients may initially maintain very good central vision. Peripheral retinoschisis occurs in about 50% of cases, and the subsequent pigmentary change that may develop may be mistaken for retinitis pigmentosa.
PRPH2 is associated with multiple macular dystrophies, including adult-onset foveal vitelliform macular dystrophy, Stargardt disease, and the pattern dystrophies. ABCA4 is most commonly associated with Stargardt disease. RPE65 is associated with retinitis pigmentosa and a form of Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA).

Q3722
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common systemic adverse event associated with intravenous fluorescein angiography?
Correct answer: A. nausea
Rationale
Nausea is the most common systemic adverse event associated with intravenous fluorescein angiography, occurring in up to 5% of patients. Hives also occur in 5% of injections.  Hypotension is very rare. True thrombophlebitis is not associated with this procedure, although fluorescein extravasation at the injection site can result in pain, edema, and erythema, which is self-limiting and treated conservatively.

Q3723
Retina & Vitreous
In which retinal cells is the response measured in the pattern electroretinogram mainly generated?
Correct answer: C. ganglion cells
Rationale
The pattern electroretinogram (PERG) shows the response of the central retina to a contrast stimulus. It is mostly generated by the retinal ganglion cells. The (full-field) ERG is not affected in patients with dysfunction confined to the macula. Patients with generalized retinal dysfunction, and thus with abnormal results on full-field ERGs, have an abnormal PERG only if the macula is involved.

Q3724
Retina & Vitreous
What cells are targeted by the cell-mediated immune response against cell antigens in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease?
Correct answer: C. melanocytes
Rationale
The cell-mediated immune response against cell antigens in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease is directed toward melanocytes. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) disease is a multisystemic disorder characterized by granulomatous panuveitis with exudative retinal detachment. It is often associated with neurologic and cutaneous manifestations. VKH disease occurs more commonly in patients with a genetic predisposition to the disease, including those from Asian, Middle Eastern, Hispanic, and Native American populations. Several human leukocyte antigen (HLA) associations have been found in patients with VKH disease, including HLA-DR4, HLA-DR53, and HLA-DQ4. Successful therapy for VKH disease is early and aggressive treatment with systemic corticosteroids, followed by local and/or steroid-sparing systemic therapy in selected patients.

Q3725
Retina & Vitreous
What imaging modality best helps determine the optimal time to surgically drain a suprachoroidal hemorrhage?
Correct answer: A. B-scan ultrasonography
Rationale
When suprachoroidal hemorrhage occurs intraoperatively, immediate drainage is rarely effective, due to rapid coagulation of the blood. Waiting 7 to 14 days often allows the hemorrhage to liquefy. B-scan ultrasonography is useful to help identify clot liquefaction. B-scan ultrasonography is also useful to determine whether "kissing," or appositional, suprachoroidal hemorrhage is present and whether concurrent retinal detachment is present. In the presence of large suprachoroidal hemorrhage, there is often no view for OCT or FA. CT is not indicated to monitor suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

Q3726
Retina & Vitreous
In the context of ocular genetic disorders, what is the definition of pleiotropy?
Correct answer: B. Diverse phenotypes share mutations in a common causative gene.
Rationale
Pleiotropy is the term for mutations in a single gene that may lead to multiple phenotypes. An excellent example of this is the ABCA4 gene, which has differing phenotypes for different mutations within the gene. The most common phenotype caused by mutation of ABCA4 is Stargardt disease (autosomal recessive, requires both alleles to harbor disease-causing mutations), but other mutations may cause pattern dystrophy, cone–rod dystrophy, or autosomal-recessive retinitis pigmentosa. Genetic heterogeneity is the term that describes multiple genes that give rise to an indistinguishable phenotype. For instance, mutations in at least 17 different genes may lead to Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA). Disorders caused by a mutation in a single allele arise from dominant inheritance. If mutations in both alleles are necessary to cause disease, then the inheritance is recessive.

Q3727
Retina & Vitreous
A patient with no prior ophthalmic history had an uneventful cataract surgery 1 week ago but now complains of blurry vision and photophobia. The visual acuity is 20/400. A hypopyon and vitritis are present. What intervention is most appropriate?
Correct answer: B. tap and inject with antibiotics
Rationale
Acute-onset postoperative endophthalmitis occurs within 6 weeks of cataract surgery and has a bacterial etiology. In evaluating the final visual outcomes for patients with acute-onset endophthalmitis and an initial visual acuity better than light perception, the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS), which was completed in 1995, found no difference between the immediate vitrectomy group and the group treated by tap and inject with intravitreal antibiotics. Chronic or delayed-onset endophthalmitis occurs more than 6 weeks after surgery and can have a bacterial or fungal etiology. Definitive treatment of chronic endophthalmitis secondary to Propionibacterium acnes may require vitrectomy with total capsulectomy and removal or exchange of the intraocular lens.

Q3728
Retina & Vitreous
What surgical practice improves the prognosis for hole closure for a stage 3 full-thickness macular hole?
Correct answer: B. peeling of the inner limiting membrane
Rationale
Peeling of the inner limiting membrane (ILM), particularly in surgeries for stage 3 and 4 macular holes, has been demonstrated to improve the rate of hole closure. Peeling of the cortical vitreous is a common feature of vitrectomy for multiple macular diseases. Vitrectomy is advised for all recent macular holes that are stage 2 or higher: Although up to 50% of stage 1 holes may close spontaneously, prompt intervention is advised for stage 2 or higher holes, given an association between hole duration and outcome. Ocriplasmin is a recombinant protease administered by intravitreal injection and designed as an alternative to vitrectomy.

Q3729
Retina & Vitreous
In the modified Scheie classification of hypertensive retinopathy, what grade is defined by the presence of obvious narrowing with some focal irregularities and arteriovenous crossing changes?
Correct answer: B. Grade 2
Rationale
Multiple systems for grading hypertensive retinopathy exist, including the modified Scheie classification, the Keith-Wagener-Barker classification, and the Wong-Mitchell classification. The Wong-Mitchell classification is a simplified version of the K-W-B system that considers the implications of retinal findings for systemic risk stratification.
The modified Scheie classification is in widespread use and is defined as:
Grade 0: No changes
Grade 1: Barely detectable arteriolar narrowing
Grade 2: More evident generalized narrowing with some focal constriction and arteriovenous crossing changes
Grade 3: Changes of Grades 1 and 2 with addition of hemorrhages, exudates, and cotton-wool spots
Grade 4: Grade 3 changes plus optic disc edema

Q3730
Retina & Vitreous
A 54-year-old phakic myope presents with an acute symptomatic horseshoe tear in the right eye. What treatment is most appropriate?
Correct answer: A. laser retinopexy
Rationale
Acute symptomatic horseshoe tear warrants prompt laser retinopexy to surround the pathology and reduce likelihood of progression to retinal detachment. Observation carries risk of progression to retinal detachment that would be unsuitable for most clinical scenarios. Scleral buckling and pars plana vitrectomy are a surgical options for eyes with detached retina, and would not typically be the preferred choice for an uncomplicated retinal tear.

Q3731
Retina & Vitreous
In a patient with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC), what characteristic abnormality, unique to this disease, can be seen on fluorescein angiography (FA)?
Correct answer: B. smokestack pattern
Rationale
FA imaging of an eye with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) may show fluorescein leakage in a pattern that resembles a smokestack. This pattern of fluorescein leakage is unique to CSC. Irregular window defects from RPE abnormalities are commonly seen, but similar-appearing changes can occur from other conditions, such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In some cases, the FA appears normal. Multifocal hyperfluorescence is not seen commonly in eyes with CSC. Lacy hyperfluorescence may be seen in rare instances, if the CSC is complicated by a choroidal neovascular membrane.

Q3732
Retina & Vitreous
A mutation of which gene in which cell type results in nonprogressive dysfunction in patients with nyctalopia and white dots?
Correct answer: D. RDH5 gene mutation in retinal pigmented epithelium
Rationale
RDH5 gene mutation in retinal pigmented epithelium

Fundus albipunctatus is caused by a mutation in the gene RDH5. RDH5 encodes 11-cis-retinol dehydrogenase, a microsomal enzyme in the RPE that converts 11-cis-retinol into 11-cis-retinal and is therefore involved in the regeneration of rhodopsin. Patients with mutations in this gene have very delayed rhodopsin regeneration, and although levels eventually normalize, the process can take many hours in the dark. Mutations in the gene RLBP1 result in retinitis punctata albescens. ABCA4 is a gene that, depending on the exact mutation, can cause Stargardt disease, fundus flavimaculatus, cone-rod dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and AMD, among others.

Q3733
Retina & Vitreous
What is the characteristic fundus appearance of dominant (familial) drusen?
Correct answer: B. drusen distribution beyond the temporal vascular arcades and nasal optic nerve margin
Rationale
A clinical feature characteristic for dominant (familial) drusen is the distribution of drusen beyond the temporal vascular arcades and nasal optic nerve margin. A single missense mutation (Arg345Trp) on exon 10 in the EFEMP1 gene of some patients with dominant drusen results in a fibrillin-like extracellular matrix protein expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina. The clinical findings typically first manifest bilaterally in the third to fourth decade of life. Although usually asymptomatic, choroidal neovascularization may develop in this patient population and lead to loss of vision.
In contrast to drusen of age-related macular degeneration (ARMD), the lesions of dominant drusen are typically small and round. Clumping and hyperplasia of the RPE and drusen clustering in the macula are features of ARMD, not familial drusen.

Q3734
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most important step in minimizing the risk of endophthalmitis when performing an intravitreal injection?
Correct answer: D. applying povidone-iodine to the ocular surface before the injection
Rationale
The pre-procedure application of 5% povidone-iodine to the ocular surface is widely considered the most important step in preventing endophthalmitis following an intravitreal injection. The patient’s conjunctiva and eyelids are presumed to be the most common source of infection. Thus, while treatment of severe blepharitis is appropriate prior to initiating intravitreal injections, excessive manipulation of the lid margin immediately before an injection may increase the release of bacteria-contaminated secretions. The benefits of periprocedure topical antibiotics is controversial, and their use is not routinely recommended. Many practices employ a workflow in which medication from a different lot number is used for each eye when bilateral injections are performed to further minimize risk.

Q3735
Retina & Vitreous
What percentage of cones overall reside outside the foveal region?
Correct answer: D. 90%
Rationale
The density and distribution of photoreceptors vary with topographic location. In the fovea, cones are predominantly red- and green-sensitive, with a density exceeding 140,000 cones/mm2. The foveola has no rods. The fovea contains only photoreceptors, rods and cones, and processes of Müller cells. The number of cone photoreceptors decreases rapidly away from the fovea, even though 90% of cones overall reside outside the foveal region. The density of rods also decreases toward the periphery.

What type of retinal detachment is associated with inflammation?
Correct answer: B. exudative retinal detachment
Rationale
Exudative retinal detachments are caused by inflammatory conditions involving the eye.

What is the etiology of Terson syndrome?
Correct answer: C. intracranial hemorrhage
Rationale

Q3739
Retina & Vitreous
What organism is associated with severe posttraumatic endophthalmitis?
Correct answer: C. Bacillus
Rationale
Bacillus

Bacillus cereus accounts for 25% cases of posttraumatic endophthalmitis, and it has a rapid and severe course that causes profound vision loss. It is associated with soil-contaminated injuries, especially those involving foreign bodies.
Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Candida are also causative organisms, although not necessarily in the posttraumatic setting.

Q3740
Retina & Vitreous
Infection with what causative organism of posttraumatic endophthalmitis results in the worst prognosis?
Correct answer: B. Bacillus cereus
Rationale
Bacillus cereus

Posttraumatic endophthalmitis due to Bacillus species infection has a dismal prognosis, owing to its rapid and severe course. Endophthalmitis develops after up to 7% of penetrating ocular injuries. Bacillus species, which rarely cause endophthalmitis in other settings, may account for up to 25% of posttraumatic endophthalmitis. E coli, Streptococcus spp, and Staphylococcus spp may lead to visual loss, but the course is typically not as aggressive as that for Bacillus spp.

Q3741
Retina & Vitreous
By what mode is the pictured disorder inherited?
Correct answer: A. autosomal dominant
Rationale
The inheritance pattern of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP/Gardner syndrome) is autosomal dominant. Gardner syndrome, also known as familial colorectal polyposis, is characterized by the presence of multiple polyps in the colon, together with tumors outside the colon. The extracolonic tumors may include osteomas of the skull, thyroid cancer, epidermoid cysts, and fibromas, as well as the occurrence of desmoid tumors in approximately 15% of affected individuals.
The ocular hallmark of this disease is the presence of a pigmented fundus lesion similar to those found in congenital hypertrophy or hyperplasia of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE). Singular lesions have little diagnostic significance and are not pathognomonic of FAP. The presence of 4 or more widely spaced, small lesions per eye and bilateral involvement suggest FAP. Lesions are often teardrop-shaped and average between 4 mm and 5 mm in size. They are usually located in the midperiphery of the fundus and exhibit autofluorescence on optical coherence tomography (OCT) testing. Atypical CHRPE is also associated with FAP.

Q3742
Retina & Vitreous
A patient complaining of recent blurring of the central vision has the retinal appearance shown in the image. What historical feature would suggest an explanatory diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. thioridazine use
Rationale
Thioridazine retinal toxicity manifests as a bilateral granular macular pigmentary disturbance that can progress to a nummular atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris.
Solar maculopathy results in a subtle, localized, parafoveal pigmentary alteration.
Hydroxychloroquine toxicity presents as bulls-eye maculopathy.
Gyrate atrophy presents with circumscribed areas of peripheral atrophy of the RPE and choriocapillaris. Carriers will occasionally have localized or mild peripheral pigmentary granularity.

Q3743
Retina & Vitreous
A 10-year-old boy presents with sudden vision loss in the right eye. The visual acuity is hand motions right eye and 20/80 left eye. A vitreous hemorrhage is apparent in the right eye. Findings of the left fundus are shown in Figure 1. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
Correct answer: D. X-linked
Rationale
The clinical presentation is consistent with X-linked retinoschisis (XLRS). The phenotype of congenital XLRS is variable, even within families. In pediatric patients, foveal schisis, which appears as small, cystoid spaces and fine radial striae in the central macula, can be best seen with optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus autofluorescence imaging. 

Central vision may initially be quite good and may remain stable for long periods, but it can eventually decline to 20/200 or worse. Peripheral retinoschisis may occur in up to 50% of patients. In severe cases involving peripheral schisis, there may be extensive areas of inner retinal elevation resembling total or subtotal retinal detachment. Histologic studies have shown that the splitting in peripheral XLRS occurs in the outer plexiform and nerve fiber layers. Boys with XLRS frequently present with vitreous hemorrhages from torn retinal vessels in areas of retinoschisis.

Q3744
Retina & Vitreous
What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of macular hole formation?
Correct answer: A. localized perifoveal traction
Rationale
It has been hypothesized that a macular hole is caused by tangential traction as well as anterior posterior traction of the posterior hyaloid on the parafoveal region. It has not been shown that macular holes are related to reduced water transport of the retinal pigment epithelium. There is no acute loss of central photoreceptors when a macular hole develops. Proliferation of glia, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), or hyalocytes at the vitreoretinal interface, especially at the posterior pole, results in epiretinal membrane formation.

Q3745
Retina & Vitreous
For a pneumatic retinopexy to be effective, the retinal breaks should be confined to what clock-hours of the retina?
Correct answer: D. superior 8 clock-hours
Rationale
Classic indications for a pneumatic retinopexy are:
  • confidence that all retinal breaks have been identified
  • retinal breaks confined to the superior 8 clock-hours
  • a single or multiple retinal breaks within 1-2 clock-hours
  • the absence of proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) grade CP or CA
  • clear media
  • patient who can maintain proper positioning

Q3746

Severe, nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy may be defined by what feature?
Correct answer: B. prominent intraretinal microvascular abnormalities
Rationale
Severe, nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy is associated with prominent intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in 1 or more quadrants. By definition, other findings include extensive (>20) intraretinal hemorrhages in each of 4 quadrants and venous beading in 2 or more quadrants. Vitreous hemorrhage is a finding in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Q3747
Retina & Vitreous
What diagnostic item is used for the evaluation of contrast sensitivity?
Correct answer: A. Pelli-Robson test
Rationale
The Pelli-Robson test measures contrast sensitivity using a single, large letter size (20/60 optotype), with contrast varying across groups of letters. Patients read the letters, starting with the highest contrast and continue until they are unable to read 2 or 3 letters in a single group. The subject is assigned a score based on the contrast of the last group in which 2 or 3 letters were correctly read. The Pelli-Robson score is a logarithmic measure of the subject’s contrast sensitivity. The anomaloscope, Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue test, and Ishihara plates are all used to evaluate color vision, not contrast sensitivity.

Q3748
Retina & Vitreous
What are typical features of acute retinal necrosis syndrome?
Correct answer: A. peripheral retinitis with circumferential spread, occlusive vasculitis, and vitritis
Rationale
Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) typically presents as peripheral retinitis with circumferential spread, occlusive vasculitis, and vitritis. Retinal breaks develop in areas of necrosis, leading to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in many cases. ARN is typically associated with vitritis. Absence of vitritis is seen in progressive outer retinal necrosis in immunocompromised patients.
Prominent anterior chamber reaction with hypopyon, macular neuroretinitis, and exudative retinal detachment are not typically associated with acute retinal necrosis. Retinal whitening and edema with a macular cherry red spot is the typical description for a central retinal artery occlusion.

Q3749
Retina & Vitreous
In what form of dichromacy is the long-wavelength (L-cone) photopigment absent?
Correct answer: D. protanopia
Rationale
Protanopia is the form of dichromacy in which the long-wavelength (L-cone) photopigment is absent. Individuals who need only 2 primary colors to make a color match have dichromacy. Such individuals lack one of the cone photopigments. About 2% of males have dichromacy; 1% are missing the long-wavelength (L-cone) photopigment, a disorder termed protanopia; and 1% are missing the medium-wavelength (M-cone) photopigment, called deuteranopia. A rare, third form of congenital dichromacy is lack of the short-wavelength (S-cone) photopigment, termed tritanopia, which is an autosomal-dominant defect that occurs in about 0.001% of the population.

What systemic disorder is associated with asteroid hyalosis?
Correct answer: A. diabetes mellitus
Rationale
Asteroid hyalosis is associated with diabetes and hypertension.
Multiple myeloma, hypercholesterolemia, and hemochromatosis are not associated with asteroid hyalosis.

Q3751
Retina & Vitreous
A 7-year-old child with congenital sensorineural hearing loss has best corrected vision of 20/60 in each eye. What would the most likely examination finding be?
Correct answer: C. retinitis pigmentosa
Rationale
Usher syndrome, an association of retinitis pigmentosa and congenital sensorineural hearing loss, is suspected in this patient. There are 3 types of Usher syndrome and all have autosomal recessive inheritance:
  • Type 1: early and profound hearing loss, RP, vestibular areflexia
  • Type 2: born with moderate to severe hearing loss and develop RP within their second decade of life but have normal vestibular function
  • Type 3: progressive hearing loss, variable RP, and sporadic vestibular function
CHARGE syndrome (association of ocular coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, mental retardation, and genitourinary and ear anomalies) patients may have coloboma and hearing loss, but this is related to middle- and inner-ear abnormalities, and these patients may have unusually shaped external ears.
Anterior uveitis is not associated with congenital hearing loss.
Cataract is associated more commonly with other forms of retinitis pigmentosa.

What premonitory symptom portends an impending central retinal artery occlusion?
Correct answer: D. amaurosis fugax
Rationale
Emboli within the carotid distribution that cause retinal artery occlusion can also cause amaurosis fugax or transient ischemic attacks.
Light sensitivity can be secondary to ocular surface diseases or uveitis. 
Flashes and floaters are associated with a symptomatic posterior vitreous detachment.
Central retinal artery occlusion is not associated with retro-orbital pain and is classically painless.

Q3753

A 40-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with an intracranial hemorrhage after a head injury. Dilated fundus examination shows vitreous and subhyaloid hemorrhage in both eyes. What is the likely long-term visual prognosis if baseline vision was normal and presuming the intracranial hemorrhage would resolve without any residual deficits?
Correct answer: D. Visual function is usually unaffected once vitreous/subhyaloid hemorrhage clears.
Rationale
The clinical vignette describes Terson syndrome. In most cases of Terson syndrome, visual function is unaffected once vitreous/subhyaloid/retinal hemorrhages clear. Spontaneous improvement generally occurs, although vitrectomy is occasionally required to clear ocular media. Timing of vitrectomy has no bearing on final visual prognosis.

Q3754
Retina & Vitreous
One month ago, a 25-year-old woman experienced transient visual loss. Two days ago, she noted a "smudge" in the central vision of her right eye. Her visual acuity is 20/40 eccentrically OD and 20/20 OS. Her pupils react briskly without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Her left fundus is normal. Given that her right fundus is abnormal as shown, what finding might be expected?
Correct answer: C. scotoma on Amsler grid testing OD
Rationale
This patient has multiple retinal hemorrhages, disc edema, cotton-wool spots, and tortuous veins from a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). The absence of a relative afferent pupillary defect strongly suggests that this is a nonischemic CRVO. However, the reduction in visual acuity would likely be associated with macular edema, which would result in a central scotoma on Amsler grid testing. A superior branch retinal vein occlusion would be associated with an inferior altitudinal defect, but this finding would not be likely in a nonischemic CRVO. In CRVO, color vision should be relatively intact. Intravenous fluorescein angiography would show delayed venous filling, staining of the retinal veins, and hypofluorescence corresponding to regions of retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots. Choroidal hypofluorescence would not be associated with a CRVO.

Q3755
Retina & Vitreous
A 20-year-old white man presents with 2 days of decreased vision in both eyes. He mentions that he enjoyed watching a solar eclipse 2 days ago. On examination, visual acuity is 20/60 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Both eyes show a yellow-white spot in the fovea. What characteristic finding on optical coherence tomography (OCT) will develop in the next several weeks?
Correct answer: C. subfoveal disruption, or loss, of layers of the outer retina
Rationale
The patient presents with solar retinopathy. The condition is caused by direct or indirect viewing of the sun for a prolonged time period. Risk factors for developing solar retinopathy include using tetracycline or psoralens (found in PUVA, which is a treatment for eczema and psoriasis), and having clear lenses. The damage is due to shorter wavelengths with high energy, such as visible blue light and ultraviolet light. Patients typically present with visual acuity around 20/40-20/100 and complain of decreased vision, metamorphopsia, central scotoma, or micropsia. Examination reveals a white-yellow foveal dot that turns into a reddish dot several days later. After 2 weeks, an outer foveal defect may develop. Fluorescein angiography is typically normal in this disease. However, in the first 48 hours, a small focal area of staining may be seen.

When evaluating a patient with vitreomacular traction syndrome for ocriplasmin injection, what ocular characteristic affects treatment prognosis?
Correct answer: A. area of vitreomacular adhesion  (VMA)
Rationale
The area of VMA is an important predictor of successful resolution of vitreomacular traction using ocriplasmin. VMA resolved in 33.6% of eyes in which the size of adhesions was 1500 µm or smaller on OCT, and in only 10.3% of adhesions larger than 1500 µm.

A patient with the fundus photograph and fluorescein angiogram shown is most likely to have what systemic disease?
Correct answer: B. atherosclerosis
Rationale
Acute central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is characterized by diffuse retinal whitening involving all quadrants, sclerotic retinal arterioles, and a cherry-red spot in the macula. An embolus in an arteriole may or may not be visible. CRAO is usually the result of atherosclerosis-related thrombosis and/or embolic cerebrovascular disease. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in patients presenting with CRAO.

Of what material is asteroid hyalosis composed?
Correct answer: B. calcium-containing phospholipids
Rationale
The characteristic small, white, round vitreous opacities of asteroid hyalosis are composed of calcium-containing phospholipids. Calcium carbonate is typically found in bone or pathologic soft tissue calcification. Collagen I and cholesterol are not found in the vitreous (secondary vitreous contains largely collagen type II).

How is "threshold disease" of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) defined?

Rationale
Initially proposed in the Cryotherapy for ROP Study and later in the Early Treatment ROP Study (ETROP), the threshold for conventional treatment is 5 contiguous or 8 cumulative clock-hours of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation (stage 3) in zone I or zone II with any vascular engorgement (plus disease).

What finding is most typically associated with vitreoretinal tufts?
Correct answer: B. focal area of vitreoretinal traction
Rationale
Vitreoretinal tufts are small, peripheral focal areas of elevated glial tissue. They are typically found anterior to the equator and often nearer the ora serrata. They are rarely associated with retinal breaks, as they often occur anterior the posterior margin of the vitreous base.

What treatment is recommended for a superotemporal meridional retinal fold without an associated retinal break?
Correct answer: C. observation
Rationale
No treatment is required for a meridional retinal fold without an associated retinal break. Such folds represent redundant retina and are typically located in the superior nasal quadrant. They may be the site of a posterior vitreous separation-induced retinal tear, with or without a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Appropriate management of these complications is indicated in that instance.

Q3762
Retina & Vitreous
A 7-year-old girl with a recent history of blunt ocular trauma is found to have a circumferential linear break without retinal detachment along the ora serrata, and an avulsion of the vitreous base. What is the preferred management option?
Correct answer: B. laser retinopexy or cryopexy
Rationale
The vignette describes a traumatic dialysis without retinal detachment in a young patient. This is best treated with laser retinopexy, or cryopexy if the view is hazy, to reduce the risk of later retinal detachment.
Close observation is an option, since the development of retinal detachment after trauma in young patients occurs most often in a delayed fashion, due to vitreous liquefaction over the tear. Thirty percent (30%) of retinal detachments after trauma are identified within 1 month, 50% are identified within 8 months, and 80% are identified within 24 months.
Treatment with encircling scleral buckle and/or pars plana vitrectomy with laser retinopexy would be indicated if a retinal detachment develops.

An ophthalmologist examines a patient who was previously diagnosed with ocular histoplasmosis syndrome. The presence of what posterior segment finding would suggest the diagnosis may be incorrect?

Rationale
Ocular histoplasmosis is characterized by "punched out" chorioretinal scars, juxtapapillary atrophic pigmentary changes, choroidal neovascularization (CNV), and the absence of vitritis. If vitritis is found in association with 1 or more elements of the classic triad of ocular histoplasmosis syndrome, then multifocal choroiditis or other uveitis should be considered as a diagnosis.

Rationale
The image demonstrates severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR). Venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) are both present and are characteristic of severe NPDR. This is not a characteristic of mild or moderate NPDR. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is characterized by the presence of retinal or iris neovascularization.

What color (wavelengths) of light is readily absorbed by macular xanthophyll?
Correct answer: B. blue
Rationale
Macular xanthophyll readily absorbs blue, but minimally absorbs yellow, red, and infrared wavelengths, so the blue wavelength should be avoided during laser photocoagulation, especially in the macula, to minimize thermal macular retinal damage.

What is a cause of severe vision loss in patients with pathologic myopia?
Correct answer: D. choroidal neovascularization
Rationale
Choroidal neovascularization is a potential complication of degenerative myopia. Following early diagnosis, this complication may be effectively managed with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy. Retinal neovascularization, retinal telangiectasis, and angioid streaks are not commonly associated with degenerative myopia.

Q3767
Retina & Vitreous
What type of identifiable cells can epiretinal membranes contain?
Correct answer: C. glial cells
Rationale
Epiretinal membranes are composed of an extracellular matrix including collagen, as well as cells derived from glia (Müller cells, microglia, and fibrous astrocytes), retinal pigment epithelium, and immune cells. The cells differentiate over time into contractile myofibrocytes. These membranes are semi-translucent and avascular. They may be idiopathic, possibly related to vitreoretinal interface abnormalities after posterior vitreal detachment, possibly allowing glial cells to pass through the internal limiting membrane and reach the retinal surface, where they can propagate as a thin membrane. Epiretinal membranes may also be associated with other conditions including retinal vascular occlusions, trauma, and retinal tears, where retinal pigment epithelial cells, exposed to the vitreous, may migrate to the macular surface. The distortion induced by contraction of the membrane may lead to reduced acuity, or the development of a macular hole (figures). Soluble factors in the vitreous may play a role in stimulating the growth of epiretinal membranes and may also provoke their contraction, leading to surface wrinkling retinopathy, macular pucker, and macular holes.

A 38-year-old HIV-positive man presents with acute vision loss in the right eye. Examination reveals multifocal areas of deep retinal opacification, involving the retinal periphery in both eyes and the macula OD. What laboratory test would be useful in establishing the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. CD4+ cell count, aqueous polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for varicella zoster virus or herpes simplex virus
Rationale
+ cell count, aqueous polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for varicella zoster virus or herpes simplex virus

The clinical description is suggestive of progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN), the etiology of which is the varicella zoster virus or herpes simplex virus. PORN occurs in immunocompromised patients, including those who are HIV positive, with a low CD4+ cell count. Although syphilis, tuberculosis, and/or a fungal infection can present with retinal involvement, multifocal retinitis of the depth and spatial distribution described above is characteristic of PORN.

Q3769

Within the retina, the density of rods is greatest at what degree of fixation?
Correct answer: C. 12
Rationale
The rod photoreceptors have their greatest density (about 160,000 rods/mm2) within the retina at around 12 degrees of fixation. Rod density decreases toward the peripheral retina. Cone density is greatest (around 140,000 cones/mm2) in the fovea. Within the central fovea, only cones are observed. The fovea is defined as a concave central retinal depression seen on slit-lamp examination; it is approximately 1.5 mm in diameter.

Aside from ingestion of cysts, by what route can ocular toxoplasmosis be transmitted?
Correct answer: D. transplacental
Rationale
Toxoplasmosis may be transmitted by ingestion of tissue cysts or by hematogenous route, which includes transplacental fetal transmission. The obligatory intracellular parasites of toxoplasmosis may not be transmitted by saliva, fomite, or respiratory aerosolization.

Q3771

A 25-year-old man reports lifelong bilateral peripheral and night vision problems, and progressive vision loss. He has no family history of eye disorders. On dilated fundus examination, there is a pale optic nerve and attenuated vessels, as well as the finding shown in the figure below. When evaluating these retinal findings, what mimicking condition must the ophthalmologist also consider?
Correct answer: D. syphilis
Rationale
The figure shows dense peripheral bone spicules, a typical fundus finding in retinitis pigmentosa (RP). When evaluating suspected RP in a patient with a negative family history (simplex RP), the clinician must consider acquired causes of retinal degeneration that can mimic RP, including previous ophthalmic artery occlusion, diffuse uveitis, infections such as syphilis, paraneoplastic syndromes, and retinal drug toxicity. Secondary forms of pigmentary retinopathy associated with metabolic or other organ system disease must also be considered.
Toxoplasmosis would not give these fundus findings, which are characteristic for RP. A diagnosis of cone dystrophy is suggested by the progressive loss of visual acuity and color discrimination, often accompanied by hemeralopia (day blindness) and photophobia (light intolerance). Ophthalmoscopy may show a symmetric bull’s-eye pattern of macular atrophy or more severe atrophy, such as demarcated circular macular lesions. Previous trauma may cause retinal abnormalities, but would not present with progressive vision loss and night blindness.

Q3772
Retina & Vitreous
What layer of the retina is formed by Müller cell footplates?
Correct answer: A. internal limiting membrane (ILM)
Rationale
The retina contains clinically relevant layers beyond its synaptic and cell body-containing layers that are identifiable by light microscopy and OCT. The ILM is formed by the footplates of Müller cells and is attached to the posterior cortical gel of the vitreous. The ILM is frequently removed during surgery for idiopathic macular holes (see Basic and Clinical Science Course, Section 12, Retina and Vitreous, Chapter 20, Vitreoretinal Surgery and Intravitreal Injections, for further discussion).
The ELM is a junctional complex, rather than a true membrane, that is formed by zonular attachments between Müller cells and photoreceptors. The MLM is located within the inner third of the outer plexiform layer and demarcates synaptic and structural associations between photoreceptors and bipolar cell processes. Like the ELM, the MLM is thus also a junctional structure, rather than a true membrane. Finally, the inner-outer segment junction (identified as the ellipsoid zone or EZ on OCT) demarcates the boundary between the inner and outer segments of the photoreceptors and reflects the photoreceptor’s status as a modified ciliated cell. The integrity of the ELM and the EZ on OCT has implications for visual acuity.

Q3773
Retina & Vitreous
A 62-year-old woman presents with metamorphopsia in her right eye. Optical computed tomography (OCT) shows posterior hyaloid causing traction, with distortion of the foveal contour and cystic changes. The visual acuity is 20/80. What management approach is most likely to result in improved visual acuity?
Correct answer: D. pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) with peeling of the internal limiting membrane
Rationale
Removal of traction with a pars plana vitrectomy has a very high rate of visual improvement. Spontaneous release of vitreomacular traction can occur but is less likely to lead to improvement in vision than PPV. Intravitreal ocriplasmin injection has been used to treat vitreomacular traction; however, its success rate is much lower than that of PPV. While triamcinolone can be used to treat many types of macular edema, it is less successful in treating edema caused by traction. Injection of t-PA is used to liquefy subretinal clotted blood and would not be beneficial in this patient.

Q3774
Retina & Vitreous
What electrophysiologic diagnostic study serves as a direct measure of macular function?
Correct answer: C. mfERG
Rationale
The mfERG is useful in the diagnosis of macular dysfunction and in assessing the extent of central retinal involvement in generalized retinal disease by producing a topographic ERG map of the central retinal cone-system function. The stimulus consists of multiple hexagons, smaller in the center than the periphery, to reflect cone photoreceptor density, each of which flashes with a pseudorandom sequence. Cross-correlation techniques are used to calculate the small ERGs corresponding to each hexagon. Overall stimulus field size is approximately 50°. The EOG assesses the health of the RPE by measuring the changes in the corneo-retinal standing potential during light adaptation. The VEP, or VER, is a measurement of the electrical signal in the brain in response to light stimulus, recorded at the scalp over the occipital cortex; it is a measure of the integrity of the afferent visual pathway. The PERG is a measure of central RGC function and is a less-direct objective index of macular function than the mfERG.

Q3775

For the condition shown, what treatment has been proven to be effective for the associated macular edema?
Correct answer: B. ranibizumab

The Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRAVO) study found ranibizumab to be an effective treatment for macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion. Patients who got monthly injections of ranibizumab had better visual acuity gain than patients receiving sham injections at 6 months.
Verteporfin is used in photodynamic therapy and is not an approved treatment for macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion. Ocriplasmin is used for vitreomacular traction and has no role in treatment of macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion. Panretinal laser photocoagulation is not used for treating macular edema associated with branch retinal vein occlusion.

Q3776

A 30-year-old pregnant woman experienced blurred vision that did not resolve when her preeclampsia was treated. Six months after she delivered a healthy girl, she had normal visual acuity, scattered defects on automated perimetry, and patchy hyperpigmentation of both fundi. What is the most likely cause of her vision loss?
Correct answer: D. choroidal ischemia during pregnancy
Rationale
The systemic hypertension of preeclampsia can cause the same lobular choroidal infarctions seen with other types of arterial hypertension. Hyperpigmentation (Elschnig spots) can be seen afterward, and the areas of infarction can cause persistent visual field defects.
Active toxoplasmosis would produce retinal whitening and vitreous inflammation. An amniotic fluid embolus could cause a branch or central retinal artery occlusion if it passed through a patent foramen ovale and could lead to altitudinal or diffuse visual field loss. Retinopathy of prematurity would not suddenly become symptomatic during pregnancy.

Q3777
Retina & Vitreous
What systemic disease is most commonly associated with endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis in North America?
Correct answer: A. endocarditis
Rationale
Endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis results from hematogenous seeding of the eye, typically during transient bacteremia. Although decreased vision and eye pain are common symptoms, many patients do not have any constitutional symptoms. A wide range of bacteria can cause endogenous  bacterial endophthalmitis. In North America, 40% of cases occur in patients with endocarditis, most typically caused by either Staphylococcus or Streptococcus species.
In contrast, 60% of endogenous endophthalmitis cases in Asia occur in patients with liver abscesses caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Nearly one-third of cases occur in patients who have urinary tract infections, most often caused by Escherichia coli. Other cases can be associated with intravenous drug use or with procedures known to produce bacteremia, particularly placement of indwelling catheters.
Clinical presentation can vary and depends on both the size of the inoculum and the virulence of the organism; it ranges from a focal chorioretinitis with little vitreous inflammation to a dense panophthalmitis that obscures the view of the posterior segment. The patient should undergo systemic evaluation for the source of infection and initiate treatment with systemic antibiotics. Additionally, intravitreal injection of broad-spectrum antibiotics should be considered.

Q3778
Retina & Vitreous
What is characteristic of retinal detachments following ocular blunt trauma in young eyes?
Correct answer: A. Retinal detachments in this setting have a delayed presentation.
Rationale
Retinal detachments following trauma in young patients typically have a delayed presentation. The delay results from the fact that the vitreous is still formed (ie, not syneretic), which has 3 effects: the formed vitreous prevents fluid movement under the retina by acting like a cork on the break; the vitreous prevents the retina from assuming a bullous shape; the progression is slow as the vitreous slowly liquefies over time. Also, trauma in younger patients more often causes retinal dialyses rather than more typical retinal tearing at the posterior margin of the vitreous base. Retinal dialyses are notorious for delay between onset and retinal detachment.

Q3779

What is the cause of retinal ischemia in retinopathy of prematurity?
Correct answer: A. absence of vascularization
Rationale
The absence of retinal vessels in the incompletely developed retinal periphery is the cause for retinal ischemia in retinopathy of prematurity. A decrease in retinal blood flow from oxygen-induced vasoconstriction may also contribute to the retinal ischemia.
Occlusion of formed retinal vessels and inflammation are not primary causes of the ischemia.
Neovascularization of the retina and vitreous are the result of ischemia, not its cause.

Q3780

What condition is a contraindication to B-scan echography?
Correct answer: D. large corneoscleral laceration

Endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, and magnetic intraocular foreign body are not contraindications for ocular ultrasonography.

Type 1 juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasia typically occurs unilaterally in young males and presents with aneurysmal dilation of the temporal macular vessels with cystoid macular edema and yellowish exudates. It is considered a variant of Coats disease and may respond to aflibercept, owing to the action of that anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agent on placental growth factor in addition to VEGF.

Q3784

What distinguishes Purtscher retinopathy from Purtscherlike retinopathy?
Correct answer: D. a history of trauma
Rationale
Purtscher retinopathy was originally described after acute compression injuries to the chest or head resulting in vision loss in one or both eyes and accompanied by findings including peripapillary cotton-wool spots, hemorrhages, and retinal edema.
Purtscherlike retinopathy refers to overlapping fundus findings that, with the exception of fat emboli from long-bone fractures, result from nontraumatic etiologies. Amniotic fluid embolism, acute pancreatitis, and retrobulbar anesthesia are all associated with Purtscherlike retinopathy. The shared mechanism of Purtscher and Purtscherlike retinopathy is thought to be injury-induced complement activation that causes granulocyte aggregation and leukoembolization that then occlude small arterioles such as those in the peripapillary retina.

Laser retinopexy or cryopexy may be indicated in patients with retinal break associated with vitreoretinal tuft. Scleral buckle surgery may be indicated if a retinal break leads to a retinal detachment.

Detachment or separation of the posterior vitreous is present in almost all eyes with idiopathic epiretinal membranes, and may be a requisite for ERM development. ERM formation is not associated with chronic hydroxychloroquine use, degenerative retinoschisis, or LASIK.

Purtscher retinopathy typically follows acute compression injuries to the thorax or head. It is thought to be a result of injury-induced complement activation, which causes granulocyte aggregation and leukoembolization. This process in turn occludes small arterioles such as those found in the peripapillary retina.

A retinal dialysis is the most common retinal defect associated with a traumatic injury. Atrophic retinal holes are most commonly associated with lattice degeneration.

Based upon the entry criteria for the EVS, the selected duration of acute postoperative endophthalmitis was 6 weeks. Acute, rather than chronic, retinopathy of prematurity is characterized by retinal neovascularization and/or antecedent tissue ("ridge"), and dilated or engorged posterior veins ("plus disease"). What is the inheritance pattern of choroideremia?
Correct answer: C. X-linked recessive
Rationale
The inheritance pattern of choroideremia is X-linked recessive. The disease is caused by mutations in the CHM gene, which is located at Xq21.2 and encodes for a geranylgeranyl transferase Rab escort protein. It is characterized by diffuse and progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris. In affected males, the degeneration initially manifests as mottled areas of pigmentation in the anterior equatorial region and macula. The anterior areas gradually degenerate to confluent scalloped areas of RPE and choriocapillaris loss. Patients have night blindness and show progressive peripheral visual field loss over 3 to 5 decades. Most patients maintain good visual acuity.

Q3794

In an asymptomatic patient with diabetes mellitus, what is the most important initial diagnostic evaluation to determine the presence of diabetic retinopathy?
Correct answer: A. a dilated fundus examination
Rationale
Several level 1, randomized, controlled studies demonstrate the ability of timely treatment to reduce the rate and severity of vision loss from diabetes (eg, Diabetic Retinopathy Study, Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study). Examination prerequisites to applying the study results are accurate documentation of the presence and severity of peripheral diabetic retinopathy and macular edema. Although the other diagnostic procedures listed are useful in the evaluation of diabetic retinopathy, a dilated macular or fundus examination is a prerequisite to determine the presence and severity of disease.
In the RAND chronic disease quality project, while administrative data indicated that roughly half of the patients had an eye examination in the recommended time period, chart review data indicated that only 19% had documented evidence of a dilated examination. Thus, ensuring timely treatment that could prevent 95% of the blindness due to diabetes requires the performance and documentation of key examination parameters. The documented level of severity of retinopathy and the documented presence or absence of macular edema assists with the ongoing plan of care for the patient with diabetic retinopathy.

In a patient with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), what is an indication to initiate Age-Related Eye Disease Study [AREDS] vitamin therapy?

Rationale
In the original AREDS and in AREDS2, participants who benefited from antioxidant vitamin and mineral supplementation were those who had either intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in 1 eye. For participants with extensive intermediate (ie, medium-sized) drusen in 1 or both eyes, 1 or more large drusen in at least 1 eye, nonsubfoveal geographic atrophy in 1 eye, or advanced AMD (ie, subfoveal geographic atrophy or choroidal neovascularization [CNV]) in 1 eye who had been assigned to the group using the combination treatment of antioxidant vitamins with zinc and copper, the rate of development of advanced AMD at 5 years was reduced by 25%. The risk of losing vision of 3 or more lines (moderate vision loss) was reduced by 19% with this combination treatment.

TIMP3

When early-onset drusen are associated with CNV in young adulthood, the diagnosis of Sorsby macular dystrophy should be considered. A 75-year-old woman with nonexudative age-related macular degeneration complains of increasing difficulty reading the newspaper since her last visit 6 months earlier. Correct answer: A. Pelli-Robson test
Rationale
Compromised contrast sensitivity can be a major functional impediment that is disproportionate to visual acuity. Traditional newsprint is a relatively low-contrast target, particularly in comparison to the high-contrast Snellen chart. The Pelli-Robson test of contrast sensitivity might produce a score indicating abnormal contrast sensitivity in this patient. Although classically used to assess night blindness (nyctalopia), dark adaptometry can also reveal abnormalities in individuals with age-related macular degeneration. These deficits, however, are less likely to be related to the patient’s current task-specific complaint. Similarly, photostress recovery time can be abnormal in patients with age-related macular degeneration, but it would be less likely to correspond to the present complaint. The Farnsworth Panel D-15 test provides a quick method of assessing color deficiency.

What complications of retinal cavernous hemangiomas require treatment?

Rationale
Retinal cavernous hemangiomas may bleed into the vitreous in rare instances. Treatment of retinal cavernous hemangiomas is indicated in cases with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage. Laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy may be used. Lipid exudation and retinal neovascularization do not typically occur from retinal cavernous hemangiomas. The lesions are static, so progressive enlargement is not expected or seen.
In contrast, retinal hemangioblastomas associated with von Hippel–Lindau syndrome can result in visually significant lipid exudation requiring treatment.

What imaging test is most appropriate in the initial evaluation of ocular trauma?
Correct answer: B. computed tomography (CT) of the eye and orbit
Rationale
All the listed tests are helpful in evaluating ocular trauma, particularly to assess for the presence or absence of an intraocular foreign body. Plain films, although still useful, might not allow visualization of small metallic or nonradiopaque foreign bodies. Ocular ultrasonography must be performed with great caution, particularly when the eye is open, as compression of the eye can lead to extrusion of intraocular content. MRI can be performed only after the presence of a ferromagnetic intraocular foreign body has been excluded and should therefore be avoided in the initial assessment. MRI offers the advantage of providing visualization of even nonradiopaque material such as wood. While a CT scan of the orbits might not allow visualization of nonradiopaque foreign bodies, it is safe to perform and should be the first choice for imaging in most cases.

Rationale
In the setting of a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), a patent cilioretinal artery that supplies the fovea specifically, rather than the papillomacular bundle in general, can spare the central macular function and allow for preservation of visual acuity of 20/40 or better. Cilioretinal arteries occur in approximately 18% to 32% of eyes and contribute to the macular circulation of approximately 15% of eyes. Anterior chamber paracentesis has not predictably been proven to improve the visual outcome in CRAO. Acute ophthalmic artery occlusion is rare and has a generally poor visual prognosis.

The history and fundus findings suggest talc emboli related to the history of IV drug use. The refractile talc particles, which have an intravascular location, do not typically cause vision loss. Rationale
Elschnig spots are a common characteristic clinical feature of hypertensive choroidopathy. They manifest as black spots surrounded by bright yellow or red halos. Elschnig spots are caused by acute hypertensive events of the choroidal vascular system, mostly in the young. These changes in blood pressure cause an infarct of the vessels, leading to atrophy of the RPE and photoreceptors they support, creating tan patches that, in time, become hyperpigmented and surrounded by margins of hypopigmentation.
Retinal hemorrhages, exudates and optic disc edema are found in hypertensive retinopathy and hypertensive optic neuropathy.

What is the most important management step in a patient who presents with a branch retinal artery occlusion?

Branch retinal artery occlusions are considered embolic events. Retinal arterial emboli have been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular mortality; therefore, emergent referral for embolic workup that includes brain imaging, evaluation of carotid arteries, and transesophageal echocardiography should be considered. Checking erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and platelets would be relevant if giant cell arteritis is suspected, but that would be less likely with a branch retinal artery occlusion. Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) and applying intermittent pressure on the globe (“ocular massage”) have been suggested but have not been found to be consistently effective in improving the patient’s visual prognosis.

Older age is not a contraindication to retrobulbar anesthesia injection. Because obesity may make endotracheal intubation more difficult, the use of retrobulbar anesthesia would be favored.

On examination, her visual acuity is 20/25 OU, her pupils react briskly without a relative afferent pupillary defect, and her color vision, confrontation visual fields, and anterior segment slit-lamp examination are normal. Rationale
The presence of superficial and deep retinal hemorrhages in the setting of an acute-onset headache suggest the possibility of malignant hypertension and Terson syndrome, which is the association of intracranial hemorrhage (usually subarachnoid) with intraocular hemorrhage. If this patient had malignant hypertension, then the clinician would also expect to see disc edema, which is absent. Subarachnoid hemorrhage may not be detected by CT scan in 10% of patients; therefore, a lumbar puncture may be necessary to diagnose her.
Carotid ultrasonography is useful when evaluating carotid obstruction, retinal artery occlusion, or ocular ischemic syndrome, none of which is present here. A vitreous tap or aspirate would show red blood cells in the vitreous, but this is already known. An orbital MRI might reveal nerve sheath hemorrhages, but it is usually normal in Terson syndrome.

Stage 0 (premacular) holes represent vitreomacular adhesion (VMA). Stage 1A holes demonstrate foveal pseudocysts with foveal traction, 1B holes represent outer breaks in the fovea. Stage 2 holes are early full-thickness holes less than 400 μm in diameter. Stage 3 holes are full-thickness holes at least 400 μm in diameter, and stage 4 holes are full-thickness holes at least 400 μm in diameter in association with a complete posterior vitreous detachment.

Q3821
Retina & Vitreous
What management has been proven to be effective in reducing the risk of vision loss from intermediate, nonexudative age-related macular degeneration?
Correct answer: D. antioxidants and zinc
Rationale
The Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) demonstrated that taking beta-carotene, vitamin E and C, and zinc reduce the rate of visual loss to advanced age-related macular degeneration (AMD) for patients with intermediate or advanced AMD in one eye. The other treatments have not been proven to be effective in randomized clinical trials, although all of the alternatives have been suggested as beneficial based upon epidemiological studies. Surveys have demonstrated that there is a significant barrier to translating the AREDS study findings, and reports have noted that up to 50% of applicable patients do not have AREDS supplements prescribed or recommended.

Q3822
Retina & Vitreous
What agent used for retinal tamponade persists in the eye for approximately 2 months after a pars plana vitrectomy?
Correct answer: D. perfluoropropane gas
Rationale
Perfluoropropane gas (C3F8) lasts for approximately 2 months in the eye after a vitrectomy and thus provides a longer-lasting tamponade than sulfur hexafluoride gas (SF6), which lasts for 2 to 3 weeks. Perfluorocarbon liquids such as perfluoro-n-octane (PFO), which are heavier than water, can be used for temporary intraoperative stabilization of the retina, but they are not left in the eye. Silicone oil must be surgically removed.

Q3823
Retina & Vitreous
An ophthalmologist is preparing to treat a 72-year-old patient for choroidal neovascularization with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy in the right eye. The left eye has confluent drusen. What would be appropriate to explain to the patient regarding the left eye?
Correct answer: C. The use of daily Amsler grid testing is needed.
Rationale
The fellow eye of an individual with unilateral neovascular age-related macular degeneration is at high risk for developing choroidal neovascularization. These patients should be instructed on daily Amsler grid monitoring. Give yourself full points if you answered "Use of AREDS vitamins is recommended" in challenge mode.
Anti-VEGF injections and photodynamic therapy are used to treat neovascular maculopathy; they have no role in treating an eye with confluent drusen without choroidal neovascularization.

Q3824
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most likely diagnosis for the fundus shown?
Correct answer: B. proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Rationale
This patient has neovascularization of the disc with nasal fibrous proliferation along the vascular arcades. Although other conditions, such as a venous occlusion, posterior uveitis, inherited peripheral retinal ischemia (eg, Norrie disease, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, and incontinentia pigmenti), may lead to this complication, proliferative diabetic retinopathy is by far the most likely and is supported by the other retinal abnormalities present, such as preretinal hemorrhage, intraretinal hemorrhage, and macular exudate. Although sickle cell retinopathy can cause neovascularization, findings are more likely in the peripheral retina.

Q3825
Retina & Vitreous
A patient reports lifelong poor night vision. The fundus examination shows numerous yellow-white dots, sparing the fovea but scattered throughout the posterior pole and mid-periphery. An initial electroretinogram (ERG) shows undetectable rod signals after a standard 30 minutes of dark adaptation, but the signals normalize in 1 eye that undergoes overnight dark adaptation. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. fundus albipunctatus
Rationale
Normalization of rod ERG responses with prolonged dark adaptation distinguishes the stationary condition fundus albipunctatus from retinitis punctata albescens. Both conditions are characterized by numerous retinal flecks, but retinitis punctata albescens is a progressive rod-cone dystrophy in which prolonged dark adaptation does not result in a full rescue of rod signals on ERG. Bone spicules may sometimes be absent in retinitis pigmentosa (RP sine pigmento), but the atrophic appearance of the peripheral retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) still differs from the discrete retinal flecks of either fundus albipunctatus or retinitis punctata albescens. As with the latter diagnosis, the ERG in RP does not normalize with dark adaptation. Fundus flavimaculatus describes a Stargardt disease phenotype in which subretinal flecks are widely scattered throughout the fundus.

Q3826
Retina & Vitreous
When administered as an intravitreal injection for retinal vascular disease, what drug is most likely to cause prolonged ocular hypertension or glaucoma?
Correct answer: C. triamcinolone acetonide
Rationale
Triamcinolone acetonide, a corticosteroid, is the most likely medication of those listed to cause a prolonged increase in intraocular pressure when administered intravitreally. The other 3 medications listed (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aflibercept) are anti-vascular endothelial growth (anti-VEGF) agents, which, as a class, are much less likely to demonstrate this effect.

Q3827
Retina & Vitreous
A 62-year-old female presents with recent-onset flashing lights and a large, ring-shaped floater in her vision. The ophthalmologist promptly diagnoses a posterior vitreous detachment. At the slit lamp, pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous are evident. A fundus examination using a binocular indirect ophthalmoscope and scleral depression is performed. Where is a retinal tear most likely to be found?
Correct answer: B. posterior edge of the vitreous base
Rationale
The vitreous is most firmly attached at the vitreous base, the optic disc margin, major blood vessels, edges of lattice degeneration, and chorioretinal scars. After a posterior vitreous detachment, the vitreous remains attached to the retina at the vitreous base, and traction on the retina can produce a tear. The most common site of retinal tears is the posterior margin of the vitreous base.

Q3828
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most likely mechanism for vitreous hemorrhage associated with laser photocoagulation?
Correct answer: A. small-diameter, high-intensity burns can perforate blood vessels
Rationale
Focal treatment with small-diameter, high-intensity burns may cause vascular occlusion or perforate blood vessels, leading to preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage.
Small spot size, high power, and short duration of applications all increase the risk of a rupture in Bruch membrane, which may give rise to hemorrhage from the choriocapillaris and development of choroidal neovascularization (CNV).
Extensive, intense photocoagulation may lead to massive chorioretinal edema and resultant serous retinal and choroidal detachment. Photocoagulation may precipitate tears of the pigment epithelium. Neither of these causes vitreous hemorrhage.

Q3829
Retina & Vitreous
What sickle cell hemoglobinopathy is most commonly associated with proliferative sickle cell retinopathy?
Correct answer: D. sickle cell hemoglobin C (SC)
Rationale
Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy occurs most commonly with sickle cell hemoglobin C (SC), at a rate of approximately 33%. It occurs less commonly with sickle cell thalassemia (SThal), at a rate of approximately 14%. Sickle cell homozygote (SS) disease results in more systemic complications but has a very low incidence of proliferative retinopathy, approximately 3%. Proliferative retinopathy is rare with sickle cell trait (AS).

Q3830
Retina & Vitreous
What toxicity is most likely to cause a cherry red spot on fundoscopic exam?
Correct answer: C. quinine
Rationale
At toxic levels, quinine can cause retinal ganglion toxicity that produces thickening and opacification of the ganglion cell layer, leading to the appearance of a cherry red spot. With time, inner retinal atrophy and optic atrophy will develop with quinine toxicity. Methanol toxicity can cause transient optic nerve head edema and macular edema, but the most common sequela of methanol toxicity is optic atrophy. Thioridazine at high doses causes a pigmentary retinopathy, while tamoxifen can induce a crystalline retinopathy.

Q3831
Retina & Vitreous
What is the appropriate timing of surgical intervention for hemorrhagic choroidal detachment?
Correct answer: C. It is postponed to allow clot liquefaction.
Rationale
Surgical intervention for hemorrhagic choroidal detachments is usually postponed 7 to 10 days to allow for clot liquefaction.
Immediate surgical intervention is not advisable, since the blood clots readily and is not easily drained.
Surgical intervention is required in cases with appositional choroidal detachments, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), or recalcitrant pain.

Q3832
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most important risk factor for the development of radiation retinopathy following plaque brachytherapy?
Correct answer: C. total radiation dose greater than 30 grays (3000 rads)
Rationale
A total radiation dose greater than 30 grays (3000 rads) is a risk factor for the development of radiation retinopathy following plaque brachytherapy. There is no definite difference in the incidence of radiation retinopathy with the use of ruthenium-106, palladium-103, or iodine-125, given equal total dosage. Pre-equatorial plaque placement does not increase the risk of radiation retinopathy, although it may increase the incidence of iris neovascularization and/or cataract. Tumors with a smaller basal diameter and apical height at presentation require a lower radiation dose and therefore potentially have a lower incidence of radiation retinopathy following treatment.

Q3833
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common risk factor for exogenous fungal endophthalmitis?
Correct answer: A. trauma
Rationale
Exogenous fungal endophthalmitis is rare in North America and Europe. In tropical regions, it occurs most commonly following trauma or ocular surgery.
Fungal sepsis, especially in the setting of systemic immunosuppression, can cause endogenous fungal endophthalmitis.
Cocaine abuse is not associated with exogenous fungal endophthalmitis.

Q3834
Retina & Vitreous
In the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS), what therapy was demonstrated to be safe and effective for the treatment of the condition illustrated?
Correct answer: A. focal laser photocoagulation
Rationale
The ETDRS demonstrated the efficacy of focal laser photocoagulation for diabetic macular edema (DME). Although intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy, intravitreal corticosteroid therapy, and vitrectomy surgery might demonstrate efficacy in the management of DME, the ETDRS preceded these therapies, and they were not evaluated in the study.

Q3835
Retina & Vitreous
Choroideremia is transmitted by what mode of inheritance?
Correct answer: A. X-linked recessive
Rationale
Choroideremia is transmitted by an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance. It is a degeneration of the choriocapillaris of the choroid, and of the overlying retinal pigment epithelium and retina. The disease results in progressive loss of vision, almost exclusively in males. In childhood, night blindness is the most common first symptom. As the disease progresses, vision loss results, frequently starting as an irregular ring that gradually expands both centrally and peripherally. Progression continues throughout the individual's life, where both the rate of change and the degree of visual loss are variable among those affected, even within the same family.

Q3836
Retina & Vitreous
Atrophic retinal holes are commonly associated with what condition?
Correct answer: D. lattice degeneration
Rationale
Atrophic retinal holes are commonly associated with lattice degeneration. They are infrequently the cause of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. They represent atrophic rather than tractional retinal breaks, so they are not caused by posterior vitreous detachment, and they are not associated with vitreous hemorrhage.

Q3837
Retina & Vitreous
Verteporfin is approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for what indication?
Correct answer: A. subfoveal CNV secondary to myopia
Rationale
Verteporfin is a photosensitizing drug that is locally activated by laser during photodynamic therapy (PDT). PDT is approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in the treatment of subfoveal choroidal neovascularizations (CNVs) associated with AMD, myopia, and presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS). The use of PDT for managing CNV has declined dramatically, given the better success of anti-VEGF agents, but it remains an adjunctive therapy for CNV in some scenarios. PDT is used off-label to treat CSC and circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas.

What is the treatment for a patient with the findings shown in the figure?
Correct answer: C. observation
Rationale
The photos represent multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS). MEWDS is characterized by the development of multiple, small, whitish, well-defined dots and spots located predominantly in the paramacular area. The symptoms and fundus findings start to improve in most patients in 2-6 weeks without treatment.

Q3839
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common cause of endogenous endophthalmitis in Asia?
Correct answer: B. Klebsiella pneumoniae
Rationale
Klebsiella pneumoniae

A wide range of bacteria can cause endogenous bacterial endophthalmitis. In North America, 40% of cases occur in patients with endocarditis, most typically caused by Staphylococcus or Streptococcus species. In contrast, 60% of endogenous endophthalmitis cases in Asia occur in patients with liver abscesses caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Nearly one-third of cases occur in patients who have urinary tract infections, most often caused by E coli.

Q3840
Retina & Vitreous
A 30-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes and mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy is worried about losing vision. What condition most acutely increases her risk of progression?
Correct answer: B. pregnancy
Rationale
Women with diabetic retinopathy must be carefully monitored during pregnancy due to the association of pregnancy with worsening retinopathy. Chronic hypertension increases the risk of progression, and the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) study, which followed patients for an average of 10 years, demonstrated that intensive blood pressure control lowered this risk. Anemia and advanced diabetic nephropathy are viewed as potential markers of advanced diabetic retinopathy.

Q3841
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common complication of pars plana vitrectomy?
Correct answer: C. nuclear sclerotic cataract
Rationale
The most common complication of pars plana vitrectomy is visually significant nuclear sclerotic cataract, developing in more than 90% of patients over 50 years of age. Retinal tears occur in less than 5% of pars plana vitrectomy cases. Intraoperative choroidal hemorrhage occurs in less than 1% of cases. Bacterial endophthalmitis occurs in approximately 1 out of 2,000 cases.

Q3842
Retina & Vitreous
What drug is associated with cystoid macular edema that does not leak or stain on fundus fluorescein angiogram?
Correct answer: C. nicotinic acid
Rationale
Nicotinic acid, a treatment for elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, in rare cases characteristically causes a cystoid macular edema that demonstrates no leakage or staining on fundus fluorescein angiography. Fingolimod, a drug used to treat multiple sclerosis, can cause conventional cystoid macular edema with typical late leakage in a “petaloid,” or flower-shaped, pattern. Similarly, rosiglitazone, a newer oral hypoglycemic agent, may cause conventional cystoid macular edema that may be confused with diabetic macular edema. Latanoprost may also be associated with angiographically positive cystoid macular edema.

Q3843
Retina & Vitreous
What is the most common cause of dense vitreous hemorrhages?
Correct answer: D. proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Rationale
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is the most common cause of dense spontaneous vitreous hemorrhages. Retinal venous occlusions and sickle cell anemia are less common causes of spontaneous vitreous hemorrhage. Posterior vitreous separation, a common occurrence, is not typically associated with a dense vitreous hemorrhage.

Q3844
Retina & Vitreous
After 15 years of diabetes mellitus and hypertension, a 62-year-old phakic man complains of 6 months of blurred vision in his right eye. Abnormalities are noted on his fundus and fluorescein angiographic evaluations as shown. What is his most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. diabetic macular edema
Rationale
The fundus has hard exudates in the macula of the right eye. The early fluorescein angiography (FA) images confirm the presence of vascular leakage and areas of capillary nonperfusion in the macula. Later images show a cystoid pattern of leakage. These findings are most consistent with diabetic macular edema. Hypertension-related retinal lesions include cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs), blot hemorrhages, lipid exudates (sometimes referred to as hard exudates) venous beading, and new retinal vessels. FA patterns of choroidal neovascularization may include classic or occult CNV or combinations of both. Classic CNV is an area of bright, lacy, and well-defined hyperfluorescence that is identified in the early phase and progressively leaks by the late phases. Occult CNV can present as late leakage from an unidentifiable source. Fluorescein angiography is relatively resistant to the optical effects of a cataract. Advanced cataract would decrease overall image quality. It is important for a cataract surgeon evaluating a diabetic patient with cataract to carefully consider diabetic retinopathy as an alternative cause of decreased vision.
